This study examines how student subgroups varied in their engagement with online mathematics modules, with data collected from Calculus and Pre-Calculus students in an Ontario university. Three main categories of student subgroups were identified: under-represented minority students, non-under-represented minority students, and students with asymptotic module completion patterns. By comparing module interaction data, we found that these subgroups exhibited distinct patterns of module activity. Additionally, we observed significant disparities in engagement between under-represented and non-under-represented minority students, with the former spending less time on modules and completing fewer activities. In contrast, students with asymptotic module completion patterns showed similar levels of engagement to their peers. Furthermore, analysis of screen activity and module completion revealed that both subgroups faced challenges completing modules, with under-represented minority students potentially benefiting from adapted design features that address existing accessibility issues.

We derive the spin-three Ward identities for Toda conformal field theories by applying the higher-spin symmetry, and then verify these identities on the lattice using a Monte Carlo study of the SU(2) Wess-Zumino-Witten model at its conformal point. We simulate the partition function and conformally-relevant four-point functions by lattice regularization, and find that our derived Ward identities are satisfied when the lattice spacing tends to zero. Our research extends the provenance of precise lattice calculations to include the spin-three case, and suggests that lattice regularization can accurately capture the properties of conformal field theories while avoiding the ambiguities associated with functional representations.

Building upon previous work, we extend the biautomatic property to a diverse range of uniform lattices within certain arithmetic groups. Specifically, we show that for numbers of positive integers $k$ and $l$, with $k$ being greater than or equal to 2 and $l$ being any non-negative integer, there exist $k$-uniform lattices within the group $Sl(l+2)$ that exhibit the biautomatic property. Additionally, we demonstrate that for certain instances of the dihedral group $D_3$, which arises from the special case of $Sl(2)$, its $3$-uniform lattices possess the biautomatic property.

Researchers explored the interaction of a scalar field with near-extremal and extremal black holes that maintain a constant mass over time, incorporating both perturbative and non-perturbative methods. When confronted with a scalar field of a specific type, near-extremal black holes behave in a manner similar to their more advanced counterparts, with both experiencing a change in their thermal profiles. In contrast, extremal black holes are found to be immune to this type of scalar field disturbance, while a analysis employing AdS/Cuscut dynamics provides them with a potential explanation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the boundary behavior of a conformal field theory mirrors the characteristics of an extremal black hole under the impact of a scalar field.

The proposed formal theory for classical reality in quantum mechanics refines the basic principles and axioms to eliminate paradoxical consequences. Initially, the set of non-classical elements was defined as being minimal and uniquely determined by applying a specific transformation to the set of classical elements. However, it has been proven that this non-minimality condition is both necessary and sufficient for defining the set of non-classical elements. Furthermore, the unique determination of the set of non-classical elements has been shown to result from the most fundamental property of the transformation - its anti-classicality axiom. The proposed research demonstrates that the set of non-classical elements can be derived from the set of classical elements through the unitary evolution described by Schrödinger's equation. The proof involves an operator transformation that maintains the minimal non-classicality and uniquely determines the set of non-classical elements from either initial or final states. The findings provide an explicit link between the proposed formal theory and quantum mechanics, thus providing a computational method for calculating non-classicality and the set of non-classical elements from either initial or final states.

Although EEG and ECoG signal decoding have shown promise in predicting walking ability in paralyzed patients, research into this topic remains limited. To address this, we developed two novel decoding approaches using EEG and ECoG signals, which effectively captured the underlying brain mechanisms related to motor function. By combining large datasets of EEG and ECoG signals, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of these methods in accurate prediction, with ECoG-based decoding proving more effective. Notably, our findings revealed that certain brain regions associated with motor control can be accurately identified even with limited training data, showcasing the robustness of our approach. These models may have significant implications for the development of targeted brain-computer interfaces in the future.

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating various entropy types and
disparity measures, which can be applied to probability distributions that cannot
be directly evaluated. Typically, entropy calculations require access to the
underlying probability distribution, but our proposed method bypasses this
requirement by utilizing only observable data. By leveraging only empirical
outcomes or independent samples, our algorithmic approach simplifies entropy
computation, making it particularly suitable for intricate probability
distributions that are difficult to handle analytically. Building upon the recent
neural network-based generation of complex probability distributions, our method
also applies the concept of training to entropy computation. Specifically, we
derive algorithms for computing different entropy types and disparity measures,
even when the underlying probability distributions are complex and cannot be written
analytically. These algorithms are demonstrated using both synthetic and real-world data.

Given a right-angled Artin group acting transitively on a tree, we demonstrate that there exists a subgraph in its vertex graph whose connected components correspond to the distinct orbits of the group's action. Additionally, if the group's action on the tree is minimal, we show that the associated subgraph separates the vertices of the vertex graph.

Graph neural networks have successfully applied graph structure representation to various tasks, but nearly all existing applications rely on static graph models. In contrast, real-world networks evolve over time, with connections forming and dissolving in a dynamic manner. This task focuses on developing a novel model called DECENNT, a neural network that learns from encodings within temporal graph windows. By combining encoder representations of nodes at specific time steps, DECENNT surpasses traditional methods representing dynamic graphs through aggregated node features and temporal graph attention networks. Experimental results show DECENNT to achieve a new level of performance on the NTU-RGBD dataset compared to previous standards.

The past decade has seen a tremendous surge in the use of stochastic processes to analyze evolutionary relationships and reconstruct phylogenetic trees. These processes, which affect molecular sequences, gene content, and synteny, often have corresponding Bayesian estimators and Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms to analyze multiple outcomes and build phylogenetic trees. As the field evolves, there's a growing need for a comprehensive overview of these stochastic processes, their underlying drivers, and the sampling events that shape microbial genomes. This survey delves into the realm of microbial genome evolution, exploring the underlying stochastic processes that shape molecular sequences, gene content, and synteny. It also highlights the Bayesian estimators and Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms used to analyze these processes, wrapping up with a look at the current research landscape and future directions for this field.

The movement of objects within an image sequence can be classified between temporary fluctuations and persistent movements. While the movement of non-living objects like vehicles is often consistent with their designated paths, the movement of biological entities like humans, animals, and seafood consistently incorporates temporary fluctuations resulting from unpredictable behaviors. Identifying and distinguishing these permanent and transient movements is crucial for developing effective models of biological trajectory. Presently, there are no existing approaches that attempt to differentiate between these two movement components. Furthermore, the existing state-of-the-art methods primarily focus on predicting the next frame or existing trajectory rather than evaluating the validity of the given trajectory. In response, we are introducing a new evaluation framework centered on distinguishing between permanent and transient movements. Specifically, we propose three assessment metrics that gauge the accuracy of models in differentiating between these two components. To complement these metrics, we also introduce a novel task of generating two separate trajectory forecasts for each given trajectory: one predicting the future based on permanent movements, and the other based on transient movements. To achieve this, we propose using intermediate agents that forecast future movements of different durations. Our experimental findings with the introduced metrics and model evaluations on created and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Our investigation reveals that the Inception Depth parameter significantly impacts the Nested Neumann algorithm's convergence rate. To mitigate the challenge of pinpointing an optimal inception depth, we introduce the Average Conjugate Gradient (ACG) method as a viable alternative. By averaging multiple Conjugate Gradient iterations with distinct inception depths, we demonstrate improved convergence across diverse inception depths, ultimately facilitating the reduction of optimal inception depth's influence on the algorithm's convergence rate.

Within complex systems, where waves intervene, it can be challenging to model and understand system behavior. By leveraging the concept of eigenchannels, which are derived from stochastic matrices, our research demonstrates that we can accurately predict the intensity patterns observed in a system near an equilibrium point. We apply this approach to analyze three different types of systems: optical waveguides, electronic transport in semiconductor structures, and nonlinear optimal transmission systems. In each case, our model successfully recreates the intensity distributions measured in a system during equilibrium by using a related stochastic matrix; this is particularly true even in scenarios where nonlinear interactions significantly impact system behavior.

Quantum Hall systems exhibit complex phase structures, and their topological characterization requires sophisticated methods. Using numerical simulations, we demonstrate that disorder-induced flat-band localization in Honeycomb and Kitaev-Shraiman-Motrunich models can be classified topologically by analyzing the bulk and boundary properties of the localized states. We propose an alternative approach to determine topological invariants directly from the disorder-affected Hilbert space. We find that this method yields the same results as other techniques and provides additional insights into the phase structures, even in the presence of strong disorders. We further show that this method allows for the identification of localized edge states in a self-consistent manner, which is a fundamental aspect of topological insulators. Finally, we investigate the relationship between this disorder-affected Hilbert space and the clean-system momentum space by performing a microscopic analysis of the localization process.

Research on the geometric properties of curves with genus one is gaining momentum, largely driven by the development of precise methods for computing their invariants. By leveraging both analytical and algebraic approaches to computing invariants, this study demonstrates the existence of distinct geometric properties in curves with genus one, with specific examples illustrating their independence. Furthermore, this research suggests that these properties can be defined independently of the method used for computation. Building on earlier work, this study also shows that the set of geometric properties in genus-one curves is countably infinite, and that each property can be associated with a unique set of curves in a genus-one family. Additionally, this research introduces a framework for defining properties based on the computation of invariants through analytic means, and provides a theoretical foundation for exploring geometric properties in higher genus curves.

Our study examines the potential for producing heavy Higgs bosons within the MSSM, focusing on the impact of complex squark parameters on the production process. By establishing a suitable phase choice, we explore how the squark effects are influenced by the phases of the stop and bottom and assess their significance in the context of the production process. Specifically, we find that the real part of the stop decay-modifying coefficient can be as high as three times its tree-level value, and the imaginary part has a notable effect on the stop-to-bottom decay width. However, we also identify that the production rate is largely insensitive to the stop and bottom phases except in the rare scenario where p p → H, H˜ are dominant processes. Instead, we find that the H, H˜ system is significantly differentiated by the stop and bottom phases in the decay H → τν and H˜ 1− → τ¯τ, providing an indication that, even with the production rates optimized, the system can be distinguished from the standard model Higgs boson by searching for the above decay channels at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of 3 ab^{−1}.

This proposed auto-correlation based test tackles the challenge of identifying structural parameters in discrete time network autoregressive models, specifically those with non-identifiable parameters. The test has the theoretical foundation to be approximately normal, and is effective even in the presence of strong network dependencies. Our method is superior to alternative tests by reducing the critical value bias, and is capable of estimating the critical value bias even in scenarios with complex network dependencies. Our analysis demonstrates that the bias of test statistics, relative to their standard normal values, can be consistently estimated without incurring significant sampling difficulties. Moreover, we find that the actual bias values are often substantial, whereas predicted values show a clear increase in bias as network dependence intensifies, exceeding initial expectations. Lastly, we apply our test to a real-world dataset, analyzing the network of best friends among a group of young children and discovering significant similarities between their network dependence structures and those associated with the US house election network.

While machine learning models generally employ stochastic gradient descent to minimize loss, certain applications involve complex, structured problems that can be solved more efficiently using alternative methods. These problems, which include optimal control, flow networks, and matrix factorization, often exhibit analytically tractable backward passes. By leveraging problem-specific structure in the forward pass, we can derive efficient algorithms for computing gradients. However, incorporating such methods into modern machine learning practice requires addressing scalability issues. To overcome these, we investigate strategies for scaling the forward pass, including using numerical methods and approximating subproblems. By demonstrating the effectiveness of these approaches on large-scale optimal control and matrix factorization tasks, we show that structured optimization can be applied to fundamental machine learning tasks even when the cost function is nondifferentiable.

Cells are composed of stress fibers that contribute to their movement and adhesion properties.
We developed a novel experimental technique to isolate and study single stress fibers
inside living cells. By using laser trap manipulation and high-speed interferometry, we could
measure the mechanical properties of these fibers as they were stretched, contracted, and
subjected to oscillations within the cells. Our measurements revealed that when stretched,
stress fibers behave like elastic proteins, but with a unique response that incorporates
both elastic deformation and sliding motions. Most notably, we found that when contracted,
stress fibers exhibit a non-linear response that is influenced by the sliding motions and
provides the basis for stress amplification. Consequently, stress fibers can withstand high
tensile forces due to their internal structure and sliding motions. Additionally, we found
that contracting stress fibers are resistant to oscillatory forces and provide a mechanism for
force retention within cells.

Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin have given rise to innovative services, shifting traditional financial systems' focus towards decentralized alternatives. To analyze the underlying transactions, researchers are using sophisticated graphical techniques. These graphs, which capture the sequence of transactions over time, exhibit cyclic patterns and offer valuable insights into potential illicit activities hidden within them. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to examining the dynamic nature of these graphs by identifying short-term cyclic behavior and measuring the duration of cycles. Our method determines the number of times a cycle reoccurs and evaluates the distance between cyclic instances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our analysis by comparing the frequency and persistence of cycles in various cryptocurrency networks, including those associated with known malware addresses. Additionally, our research highlights the difficulty of distinguishing legitimate from illicit activities based on cycle statistics alone, despite cyclical patterns providing a foundation for further exploration.

A pressing issue arises during coherent quantum computations: error correction. Ranking the importance of measurement outcomes is a crucial initial step. Conventionally, this ranking is achieved through carefully designed protocols, such as the Pauli channel expansion or the quantum asymptotic error correction expansion. However, these methods solely consider the average error rate and offer limited insight into the performance during individual runs of the experiment. This knowledge gap can be addressed by the development of efficient decoding strategies that learn from experienced teammates. Utilizing reinforcement learning, such as Q-learning or deep double Q-learning, enables the derivation of value functions that prioritize measurement outcomes based on their impact on the overall error correction process. Through the application of deep neural networks to raw encoder-state data, the derived value functions can be learned without the need for a complex quantum engine simulator. As a result, even if the final measurement outcome does lead to correction, the learned approach can anticipate this outcome and prioritize alternative actions that could lead to a more desirable outcome, such as recovering the original quantum state.

Quantum metrology investigates how using quantum-mechanical systems can precision-measure physical parameters. A key concept in this field is the quantum compass, which determines the direction of a physical entity based on quantum sensing. Here, we explore a quantum jump metrology approach for this task and find that it offers improved performance when measuring rapid changes. Our method involves monitoring the duration between spontaneous photon emissions from a system of interacting atoms trapped within a cavity. This is contrasted with more conventional methods, such as using the total number of photons emitted or the difference between two independent measurements. Our approach requires the fewest possible number of photons and the fewest system components needed to achieve the highest accuracy.

Our research examines the production of hadrons in Au+Au collisions, specifically how it varies with the quark's momentum fraction. Due to the limited accessibility of anti-diquarks, we focus on quark production and utilize lattice QCD simulations to determine the distribution functions, as defined by the twist-2 quark matrix elements. These results were obtained using lattice ensembles with 2.8--3.4 ge 10^(-2)å and N_t = 4, and our findings demonstrate the untypical behavior of quark distribution functions u(x) and ñ(x) as x decreases. As x decreases from its initial value, u(x) and ñ(x) first increase, then exhibit a typical decrease seen in perturbative QCD. Our analysis reveals that the increase in u(x) and ñ(x) as x decreases can be attributed to the influence of the sigma term. Furthermore, we found that the ratio of ñ(x)/u(x) fluctuates in a positive manner with increasing x. These findings are consistent with experimental data from the PHENIX and STAR collaborations, and our predictions for various hadrons show that the increase in u(x) and ñ(x) as x decreases holds true across different quark flavors.

In 1918, Hardy and Littlewood proposed a method for finding upper bounds for integer sequences of the form ${n^it(n)}$, where $t(n)$ represents the number of options for each $n$th positive integer. We have expanded on this approach by developing a more general strategy for estimating upper bounds for sequences of the form $\sum_{n \leq x} a_n^2 = Kx + O(x^{1/2})$, where $a_n$ follows a specific pattern and is determined by a set of given parameters. By applying our proposed method to Euclid's classic sequence, we have derived a more efficient upper bound for the number of gaps in the set of square-free numbers than previously known methods. Additionally, our approach enables a similar improvement in the search for gaps in the set of powers that are congruent to $1$ modulo a prime number.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in high-performance computing that leverage cloud technology, addressing latency and bandwidth challenges in cloud-based HPC systems. To facilitate efficient cloud-HPC deployments, we outline key considerations for application developers, cloud providers, and HPC administrators. We also examine the current state of cloud-HPC services, highlighting performance-enhancing strategies that proactively manage workload scheduling, data placement, and memory optimization. To move forward, we highlight several research opportunities and suggest a performance benchmark suite specifically designed for cloud-HPC environments.

This research addresses the complex contextual linear bandit problem, where the context and an action's outcome share a shared latent structure. We introduce a novel variable distribution learning method that considers the context's knowledge impact on outcome data. This approach allows us to establish tight bounds on the expected number of samples needed to learn the context distribution and the underlying structural parameters with any given level of accuracy. Additionally, this method enables us to establish a linearly scaled, logarithmic sample complexity for regret minimization in the contextual linear bandit problem, where the context and outcome data have different dimensions. Our approach incorporates a new separation of data into two parts for learning the context and outcome distributions and using this knowledge to select actions and estimate parameters. Our results show that our approach can achieve the same level of efficiency as methods that learn the context and outcome distributions simultaneously. However, our approach offers more flexible generalization, which is essential for addressing the complex contextual linear bandit problem.

Our research seeks to address the complex issue of how the rise of remote work has influenced Scrum implementation and project success. While numerous studies have investigated the link between Scrum and success, our analysis centers on identifying variables that influence this connection and their interaction with working remotely. We utilize a survey-based approach, collecting data from software development professionals with Scrum experience and employ statistical methods to analyze the results. Our data analysis yields insights into the relationships between these factors and how they are affected by remote work, alongside practical suggestions for enhancing project success through tailored Scrum implementation strategies.

We investigate using approximate value functions to accelerate policy learning with a sample-efficient model. Specifically, we analyze whether a simplified value function approximation, obtained by training a linear model on test samples, is sufficient to effectively guide policy parameter optimization. Our results demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach yields a viable alternative to more complex value function approximations, even in challenging scenarios. We propose a compact, linear value function model and demonstrate its performance in rigorous experiments, showcasing significant speedups in policy learning with minimal compromise on performance. Our findings validate the practical applicability of this model and provide actionable insights for optimizing value function approximations.

This study presents detailed investigations into the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, specific flavored hadrons (pions, kaons, and protons), and their vocational symmetry in 5.02 TeV lead-lead collisions. Our analysis reveals how these distributions relate to elliptic flow patterns and reveals subtle differences in pion, kaon, and proton transverse momentum distributions as a function of centrality in collisions. Furthermore, this study explores the balance of elliptic flow and particle production in heavy lead ion collisions, uncovering intriguing variations with kinetic energy and centrality.

This paper defines the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform and proves related inequalities, including Heisenberg's Inequality, the Quadratic Melnikov Inequality, the Bessel Inequality, the Hardy Inequality, the Power Mean Inequality, and the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, among others. Additionally, the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian cases of these inequalities are explored.

This research explores binary power control in high-interference wireless networks, focusing on a key variation where some users have access to network-wide interference information. Binary power control is modeled as an extensive form game, where each user chooses whether to use their transmission device based on whether their signal is received with low or high interference. We proven that in this game, the equilibrium payoffs are similar to those achieved by optimal power control, with only minor losses. These findings are confirmed by simulations and show that even in large networks, the average payoff can approach the optimal payoff. Notably, having access to network-wide interference information does not significantly improve payoffs in high-interference networks.

This study introduces a new multiple-time-step integration scheme (MTSA) in the discrete element method (DEM) for simulating particle-laden flows. By separating the movement of particles into distinct time steps, incorporating both short and long periods, the algorithm enhances the computational efficiency of simulations. A key aspect of the method is the inclusion of an intermediate step that models fluid-particle interactions, allowing for precise calculation of the fluid's influence. A key benefit of the method is its ability to balance computational speed and accuracy. The algorithm was tested by simulating a simple scenario of freely falling particles and comparing the results to both traditional DEM and a highly refined versions of the algorithm. The findings indicate that the average error in particle position is reduced by up to 50% when using the new algorithm, without needing to double the computational time.

We provide a new expression consisting of $7^n$ as the product and using only two positive integers in the form of $a$ and $b$, with the constraint that their sum equals $7^n$. This novel representation utilizes the properties of recursive sequences related to the Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, and it offers an innovative approach to writing $7^n$ as a sum of two powers of 7, where the exponents increase in a specific pattern. Additionally, this discovery leads to a refreshing new outlook on the relationship between numbers in the form of $a$ and $b$ that sum to a power of 7, and it suggests that similar scenarios might exist for numbers in the form of 2 or other small primes raised to a power of $n$.

We developed a feedback control system that helps a robotic hopper navigate through complex paths while moving at a constant speed, and tested it on the University of Colorado's soft-rotten "marshmallow" surface. Using a 3D simulation and quick computer processing, we designed the system to minimize errors between the robot's actual and intended movements. Testing the system on the soft surface with a fast computer and simulated movements, we found that it effectively reduced tracking errors. When the system was tested on the actual surface with a slower computer, but with the same movement it had simulated, the feedback control system helped the robot stay on track, although it didn't reduce the errors as much as it had in the simulation.

Using a hypercentral potential model, we have derived the wave functions and corresponding charge radii for mesons consisting of heavy quarks and light cones or discs of charge. The potential model incorporates a screening effect from the creation of quark-antiquark pairs and takes the form $-g\frac{\vec{\Gamma}\cdot\vec{\Gamma}}{r}$, where $\vec{\Gamma}$ represents the Fock-Schwinger representation of the quark momentum. We have also considered two types of mesons: those with point-like distributions of charge, described by Dirac delta functions located at the quark and antiquark positions, and those with charge distributed in disc shapes, described by the Thomas-Fermi model. Our calculations yield the same potential for all mesons and demonstrate that the charge radii of these mesons are directly proportional to the inverse of their masses, in agreement with experimental observations.

The effects of significant twisting movements of a droplet on the transfer of heat and mass in the surrounding gas were measured using a droplet located within a sealed chamber, where changing the airflow speed and temperature allowed for experiments to be conducted over a broad range of conditions. By using two different methods to analyze the data, it was possible to study both small and large droplet movements. For smaller droplets that move minimally, a established boundary layer model matches the measured results. However, for larger droplets that undergo substantial movement, the surrounding gas forms a turbulent boundary layer, and the measurements cannot be fit using either simple boundary layer models or more complex models that account for wave motions.

Although negation is a crucial element in natural language and has far-reaching consequences, there is limited research on negation-related tasks despite the availability of extensive linguistic data. To address this, we introduce two evaluation tasks: predicting the presence of negation and classifying the scope of negation. These tasks are significant because they involve more than just identifying negative language; they require an understanding of contextual meaning. Additionally, they involve multiple possible interpretations and demand higher levels of linguistic proficiency. Our study utilizes the LINGPAIL dataset, which comprises 340k training examples and 10,000 testing examples derived from Wikipedia articles and annotated by multiple human judges. The evaluation shows that even using highly advanced neural network architectures like BART and T5 on these tasks is challenging, and the results do not differ significantly from baseline models. However, our experiments indicate that these state-of-the-art models perform better than earlier models and achieve a level of performance close to human judges, with an F1 score of 83.5% in predicting the presence of negation and a micro- F1 score of 75.2% in determining the scope of negation.

The analysis of complex information networks typically focuses on localized, detailed examinations within specific topic domains. These examinations are often individualized, unconnected, and lack the context necessary to fully understand the network's structure and topic distribution. A proposed method, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizes a hierarchical structure to model information networks and their corresponding document topics. This approach wraps core topics in a higher-level meta-topic framework for better preservation of topic hierarchy. Furthermore, HDTM successfully integrates local topic details with the higher-level meta-topic structure through a hierarchical exchange of information. Experimental results using both real and simulated data demonstrate the effectiveness of HTDM in identifying topic hierarchies and outperforming alternative methods for predicting network structure.

Quantum annealing is a heuristic for solving combinatorial optimization problems by finding a minimum of a Hamiltonian, starting from a trivial ground state, by gradually changing a parameter. This process is known as the quantum annealing schedule. Research has shown that there is an "annealing gap" - the difference between the quantum annealing success probability and classical annealing success probability - which can be understood by analyzing the schedule. In this study, we propose a new protocol, called the incremental annealing protocol (IAP), which closes the annealing gap for any given schedule, while remaining within the realm of quantum annealing. We demonstrate that IAP can solve combinatorial optimization problems with a gap of at most $2^{-n}$ for binary Hamiltonians. Additionally, we examine the application of IAP to two specific problems: the exact cover problem and the binary integer programming problem. Findings indicate that IAP outperforms existing quantum annealing protocols, resulting in success probabilities of 1 for instances with $n\le 7$.

This research introduces novel methods of aligning process execution sequences, namely infix and postfix alignments, along with corresponding metrics to assess these alignments. Conventional alignment techniques are shown to have limitations in capturing the temporal dynamics of system calls, leading to the development of new methods that can handle partial order processes. An experimental analysis of system call sequences reveals that infix and postfix alignments provide more precise insights into system behavior, offering a new perspective on process execution evaluation.

To understand and control the magnetic and superconducting properties of nickelates, it's crucial to study their fundamental material properties. We investigate the electronic structure of epoxy-assisted aligned nickelate films using spectroscopic techniques and computational modeling. Our results show that these films possess exceptional crystal clarity and electrical conductivity. The observed band configurations and related electronic interactions are examined in detail, revealing the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling and competing magnetic interactions that may stabilize superconductivity. Additionally, our analysis highlights the potential for these competing interactions to be manipulated through applied strain, offering a means to control the nickelates' electronic structure and ultimately their magnetic and superconducting properties.

This study examines decay patterns in solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation, with a focus on collision kernels that contain a singularity and may not restrict velocities to a finite range. By using a recent framework for nearly-conservative solutions and applying the bilaplace operator, we explore initial conditions and velocity interactions influencing decay rates. Specifically, we find decay rates controlled by the singularity of the collision kernel, with influences from both short- and long-scale velocity interactions, and confirm predictions through numerical simulation and analytical evidence. Notably, when the collision kernel has an singularity of $|u-v|^{m}$, with $m$ being any real number, the solution decays in a time-scale of $N^{2-m}$ for any positive number N, confirming our theoretical findings.

Using a large dataset of wind-generated waves from the Eastern North Pacific, we used a high-resolution model to analyze how wind speed affects the shape of wave slopes probability distributions. Even at high wind speeds, we found that the distributions remain symmetric, contradicting earlier research findings. Additionally, we observed how wind speed, hurricane force, and storm direction influence the shape of these distributions. Our analysis reveals that wind speed has the greatest impact on wave shapes, with asymmetry increasing in tail regions as wind speed rises. Notably, we discovered that wave slope asymmetry is predominantly driven by wind, rather than storm direction or force, indicating that wind plays the most significant role in shaping wave asymmetry.

Over time, software systems undergo significant evolution, causing their source code to become increasingly complex and prone to errors. To tackle this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods to preserve the dependability of these systems by identifying relevant dependencies in their source code. One such approach involves constructing a matrix from the source code's abstract syntax tree, which effectively captures the dependencies between modules. However, this approach is often hindered by changes in the system's evolution, which can make it difficult to utilize existing research findings. To address this issue, this study introduces an innovative application of singular value decomposition (SVD) to decompose the matrix into two components: a compact representation of the underlying structure and a set of singular values that indicate the magnitude of each row and column in the matrix. By utilizing this compact representation, researchers can easily demonstrate, verify, and validate the reliability of software systems by analyzing their module dependencies. Furthermore, this approach enables rapid detection of critical modules, and the ability to establish a minimum set of modules required for the system's basic functionality. The proposed method has been implemented in a tool called SVD-PS, which is made available for public use through its online repository.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to numerous widespread infections and severe consequences, also affecting the global economy. To combat the spread, various countries implemented strict lockdowns and multiple restrictions. As the pandemic's impact was unparalleled, people turned to social media to seek reliable information and express their opinions. This study examined public perceptions and sentiment patterns on Twitter in relation to COVID-19 and the associated lockdowns in India. With a focus on the key lock-down period from March 20 to April 20, 2020, we collected and analyzed relevant data, applying machine learning techniques to extract essential information and evaluate sentiment. Our analysis revealed the top sources of influence on Twitter, along with the most frequently used hashtags, and examined sentiment changes over time. Furthermore, we identified the optimal model for sentiment analysis using machine learning and found that locked-down individuals displayed more positive sentiments on Twitter, likely due to reduced stress levels.

Despite decades of research, the mechanism behind cuprate superconductors' low-temperature transition remains unclear, though interlayer coupling is likely responsible. An intriguing phenomenon observed in these materials is the variation in intralayer and interlayer coupling strengths with phyical distance. Studies have typically focused on interactions within the copper oxide plane and have used in-plane measurements to estimate the strength of isostropic intralayer coupling. In contrast, the strength of interlayer coupling, obtained from out-of-plane measurements, has shown a more pronounced influence on the superconducting transition and varies significantly with the angle of misorientation. As a result, it is proposed that the average intralayer coupling is insufficient to drive the high-to-low-temperature transition on its own, while the most critical factor is the anisotropic interlayer coupling. Supporting this idea, studies have shown that the dependence of interlayer coupling on misorientation is reflected in the shape of the superconducting dome in pressure-temperature space. Furthermore, the variation of interlayer coupling with misorientation is linked to the direction of heat flow, supported by thermal Hall conductivity measurements in H$_{2}$O-doped Cu$_{2}$CdGe$_{3}$O$_{2.5}$ and H$_{2}$O-doped Cu$_{2}$RhGe$_{3}$O$_{2.5}$. The characteristics of quark stars are significantly impacted by the presence of a deconfinement phase transition, especially if it's abrupt, which can result in a distinct density gap. This study examines the effect of a continuous transition on these stars, using a linear model that incorporates temperature's impact on the equation of state. The model displays a cross-over behavior characterized by a sound speed near the critical temperature that exceeds the speed of light, which can be a potential constraint for quark star research. Additionally, this study investigates how the adiabatic index varies with density and temperature within the cross-over region, demonstrating that it exceeds 4 across the entire quark phase. As a result, quark stars would always have first-order phase transitions if the cross-over behavior isn't considered. Conversely, quark stars might exist without such transitions, which could result in neutron-star-black-hole mergers producing quark stars rather than neutron stars. Finally, this research suggests that the unique features of quark stars, including the density gap and strange quark matter, may be attributed to the cross-over's influence on the equation of state, which could result in quark stars having higher masses than neutron stars.

This research paper investigates the fundamental concept of Tai distance and mapping in unordered trees, introducing novel variants of Tai mapping and distance measures for binary trees. It demonstrates that determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is akin to solving the longest common subsequence problem, with a time complexity of O(n^2), in contrast to the anti Tai mapping, which can be solved in O(n) time. Additionally, the paper shows that calculating the maximum-weight Tai mapping corresponds to finding the longest common subsequence, while the minimum-weight Tai mapping is analogous to finding the shortest common subsequence. It further implies that Tai distance between two trees is equivalent to the weight of the maximum-weight Tai mapping. The paper also presents dynamic programming solutions for computing maximum-weight and minimum-weight Tai mappings, as well as anti Tai mappings, and demonstrates the efficacy of these methods through experimental evaluations.

Quantum metrology investigates how measurement interventions enhance the precision of physical parameters. This study examines the standard method of estimating rotation damping, $\gamma$, in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with a compass state, specifically its variance, $V_\gamma$, and finds that it is not maximized when the rotation damping is unknown. Instead, it reaches its highest point when the state is highly entangled and varies greatly with the rotation damping, $\gamma$. When the state is well-conditioned and robust to noise, the estimated variance is minimal. The results imply that the estimated damping, $\hat{\gamma}$, is accurate with little bias. Therefore, entangled states that exhibit minimal variance in estimating rotation damping can effectively estimate other unknown parameters in a balanced beam splitters experiment.

New evidence suggests that a significant amount of dust is present in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, which could be responsible for the observed infrared excess. A model developed previously, which accounts for dust effects, revealed that a protoplanetary disk with a gas phase and lingering dust particles could efficiently cool down in the outer regions. Despite this, it remains unclear how dust influences the disk's overall cooling rate. By incorporating the model's dust effects into a unified model of protoplanetary disks, we found that dust has a minor impact on the cooling rate in the inner regions but significantly accelerates cooling in the outer regions. This distinction arises because the dissipation of shear turbulence is hindered by the presence of dust in the outer regions, whereas gas collisions dominate the cooling rate in the inner regions. As a result, dust influences the disk's overall cooling rate by less than a factor of two, except in the outer regions where gas temperatures exceed 200K and dust has a more substantial impact.

This study examines the behavior of harmonic functions within a certain type of geometric framework known as gradient shrinking Ricci solitons. Our research reveals a new estimate for the growth of such harmonic functions, which holds a greater dimensionality than previous estimates and may be expressed in terms of the soliton's potential function. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the dimensionality of harmonic functions and the soliton's type, specifically its soliton dimension, which represents the largest dimension for which the soliton's potential function displays a linear growth pattern.

In machine learning models, a reliable attack known as the backdoor attack has been created, allowing the compromise of certain data inputs in a specific task. However, existing research on building a durable backdoor that functions across multiple tasks is limited due to the difficulty of maintaining consistency across labels in high-dimensional datasets. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel attack that modifies the model's behavior based on the input's embedding features rather than its label. By manipulating the model using adversarial optimization, we insert a persistent backdoor that affects multiple classification tasks. Our experiment shows that this attack is successful even if the trigger is placed in a hidden region of the input space, and that it can be implemented in image classification, text classification, and more complex datasets like Graph classification. Compared to a traditional label-based backdoor, our attack is more difficult to discover and can be implemented in high-dimensional datasets more easily.

These measurements allowed us to determine the planet's orbital path with great accuracy and identify any variations in the star's proper motion. For UY Sex 'b', we discovered that its movement isn't directly aligned with the star's movement and that its own motion is affected by its massive presence. Furthermore, we discovered that its movement is affected by its massive presence and that its own motion isn't directly aligned with the star's movement. The effects of viewing the system from an angle also became apparent as we noticed a distortion in the planet's observed motion that is linked to its position. The more the planet is offset from the edge of its orbit, the greater the distortion viewed from the side. This distortion results in a shift in the measurement of the star's distance from a maximum of almost 0.5 parsecs. This effect varies depending on the viewer's angle and reaches its greatest at points that are 90 degrees away from the Earth's orbit around the Sun. Researchers have been utilizing data-driven methods to decrease model complexity in dynamics with significant nonlinear interactions, often relying on autonomous systems. The reduction techniques typically employed, such as the method of modes or proper decomposition, are linear and therefore inadequate for complex systems. The development of nonlinear reduction techniques, specifically those utilizing artificial neural networks, is more recent. Currently, training these deep learning-based models is limited to small, linear models and there is a lack of studies applying them to complex nonlinear systems. This study introduces two novel algorithms for reducing complex nonlinear models and demonstrates their effectiveness in a classic example of a nonlinear system, the Rayleigh-Benard convection. The models are trained using the proper decomposition technique and deep network modeling, and we show that using deep learning significantly improves the results by significantly reducing the required computational power. Specifically, using deep learning enables the reduction of models with millions of degrees of freedom to a manageable level, achievable only with models in the thousands using more traditional techniques. Additionally, the results point to further potential efficiency gains as costs for training these complex models continue to drop.

In a dual Bose-Einstein condensate, we investigate how two types of solitons, with positive and negative effective mass, interact when presented with a force that causes them to move in opposite directions. Our study reveals that by adjusting the strength of this force, we can either avoid collision, observe a typical merger of solitons, or even witness solitons bypassing each other. Furthermore, we explore how this interaction affects the stability of the solitons and identify specific boundaries beyond which they become unstable. Our research utilizes a method of dual variables to simplify the complex physics, allowing us to derive an intuitive model that accurately reflects the underlying physics.

This research introduces a homomorphic parallel computation technique using a novel coding method that significantly reduces the amount of communication between nodes. By leveraging AMD Zen3 chips and developing an appropriate coding framework for encoded integers, we've achieved major advancements in efficient secure machine learning inference. Our method involves two main components: encoded integer representation and "rotor-based" encryption. We've also created a set of secure rotation functions that can be executed in parallel, which has a notable implication - our approach makes homomorphic parallel computation more practical for a wide range of secure ML applications, even with a single-user setting. To further improve performance, we've developed an approximate integer decomposition method that reduces computation costs in certain secure ML tasks. Our prototype has demonstrated outstanding results, with notable improvements in energy efficiency, computation speed, and secure ML training. For example, our secure training of a ResNet50 model with 150 layers and 2 million parameters requires only 0.23 seconds and 0.92 joules on an AMD EPYC 7776, a significant improvement over previous methods.

We've discovered new HI clouds associated with the Milky Way and surrounding Great Wall structure, which are linked to the M31 galaxy. These HI clouds span nearly 700,000 miles when viewed from the Earth's perspective and are situated approximately 800,000 light-years from the Milky Way. Observations indicate that the HI clouds move at a speed of approximately 45,000 miles per second, which is the same as the speed at which the M31 galaxy is approaching our galaxy. According to computer simulations, the M31 galaxy is on a collision course with the Milky Way due to their shared movement within a common potential gravitational field. The M31 galaxy's gravitational influence is causing the HI clouds to rotate rapidly and the surrounding matter to be drawn towards it. The computer simulations last around 8 billion years and cover an extensive area of nearly 1.7 million light-years. The findings challenge current understanding of nearby spiral galaxies and their dynamics. The discovered HI clouds provide a better understanding of how galaxies are structured and the computer simulations allow for more accurate predictions about the cosmic mergers that our galaxy will experience in the future.

The incorporation of external knowledge into knowledge-based question answering (KB-QA) systems is commonly done through a semantic analysis of the input question, which pinpoints relevant knowledge to retrieve from an external knowledge base and generate an accurate response. Nevertheless, the usual practice is to combine semantic analysis and response generation using static syntax-based models that are both limited in understanding the meaning of the input and the generation of sophisticated responses, and require massive amounts of labeled data. This research takes a different approach by utilizing deep learning models that naturally excel at capturing the meaning of input information and producing complex outputs, but are typically used in natural language processing tasks like KB-QA. To overcome the challenge of incorporating external knowledge, we propose a novel technique that leverages a semantic-driven approach, which guides the attention of the model towards the most relevant knowledge during inference. By integrating this approach with attention-based neural models, such as neural semantic parser and neural KB-QA models, we achieve significant performance enhancements and improve the efficiency of inference. Moreover, our proposed technique allows for straightforward incorporation of new knowledge into the system without needing to retrain the model.

Developing comprehensive theoretical models for small oxygen-containing cations like CO2+, NO2+ and O22+ is complicated due to the high energy requirements and the absence of clear spectral signatures. Nevertheless, a recent study employing advanced optimization techniques and multiconfiguration wave functions has successfully mapped these molecules across their energy spectra. By applying a combination of complete internal contraction and immersion methods, the multiconfiguration time-dependent self-consistent field approach has yielded accurate results for these complex ions, even in their ground states and at low energies. The proposed method has been applied to create potential energy curves in grounds and excited states for CO2+ and NO2+, as well as to obtain adiabatic electron detachment energies for O22+. The findings from this study are also compared with existing results obtained through other numerical methods.

We introduce a straightforward algorithm to decompose any element in a global domain of characteristic not two, or a global domain of characteristic two with the unique residue field being a local domain, into the sum of a square and a product of two elements from the domain's U-factored ideal.

We suggest utilizing the electric field correlation function, specifically its lag, 
as an effective new variable to distinguish between jetted and thermal neutrino emissions 
from compact binary mergers. We develop a general relativistic, 3D neutrino model that 
enables the calculation of this new variable for post-merger neutrino emissions from 
binary neutron star mergers. We examine the characteristics of neutrino signals for various 
orientation angles, the effects of general relativity on the neutrino field, and how 
neutrino emission is influenced by the presence of an accretion disk. Additionally, 
we explore the capabilities of present and future neutrino detectors using this new 
variable and find that it could significantly enhance the sensitivity of these detectors 
in detecting neutrino signals from binary neutron star mergers. With this new variable 
and detection strategy, we anticipate improved sensitivity to neutrino energies below 
10^51 erg, which is a critical area for neutrino astrophysics.

Evaluating the performance of relational machine learning models, particularly when they are used for pharmacology, a highly interlinked domain, poses a significant challenge. This challenge stems from the extensive connections between drug compounds, target proteins, and their interactions, which necessitates consideration of multiple aspects to achieve accurate evaluation. In our study, we tackle this challenge by presenting a novel evaluation framework that accounts for both relational and predictive aspects of model performance. This framework complements existing evaluation techniques and incorporates metrics that are appropriate for pharmacology, such as mean absolute error and mean squared error, in addition to considering the consequences of prescribing drugs based on the model's predictions, even if they are inaccurate. Furthermore, wecomplement our framework with a set of best practices that are designed to facilitate training and evaluating the performance of relational machine learning models in pharmacology, making it easier for researchers to reproduce and build upon our findings.

The work presented in this paper contributes to multiple research advancements within the field of rough paths. It begins with an improvement to the Young integral, specifically regarding its upper bound in the norm. This improvement facilitates the extension of the Young integral to monotone tractable functions, even in the presence of $\alpha$ close to 0.5. Another significant contribution involves the convergence of rough path signatures, which provides a basis for further exploring deep learning in the context of rough paths. Finally, this paper presents a new analysis of the truncation operator for rough paths, including an upper bound for its norm and its adjoint, which enables the derivation of new bounds for the increased complexity operator.

Despite the significant potential of machine learning to solve complex problems, its full realization depends on efficiently handling large datasets across multiple locations. However, training models from distributed data often requires them to be centralized, which can be costly due to communication limitations. To tackle this challenge, we've developed a novel decentralized method that utilizes a random walk algorithm to assign a static model to a network of nodes for ongoing training and refinement. During this process, model parameters are averaged to minimize interference, and a decentralized clock is used to determine when to update models. When tested on a decentralized dataset within a simulated network, our approach demonstrated not only energy-efficient training but also a notable enhancement in accuracy compared to a centralized model. Furthermore, we found that our method facilitates seamless cloud integration.

Inertial wave turbulence was observed and analyzed in the Euler fluid dynamics using a non-dimensional parameter. The resulting energy spectrum matches the $k^{-3}$ slope, and this study confirms that the correct parameter for studying inertial wave turbulence is the Kubo number. For geophysical turbulence, the Kubo number is low, and the research indicates that the energy spectrum remains at $k^{-3}$ throughout. However, the energy spectrum transitions to $k^{-5/3}$ in high Kubo number scenarios, and this transition can occur even if the Coriolis force becomes weaker. The research also reveals that the energy spectrum can be accurately modeled using a $\frac{5}{3}$ exponent after the transition, and this study also explores the conditions under which the energy spectrum transitions back to $k^{-3}$.

Mental health disorders exert a significant influence on crime rates, with certain illnesses such as schizophrenia having a profound impact on both the individuals suffering from it and the communities affected by it. Despite the numerous initiatives aimed at providing mental health treatment within the penal system, providing effective treatment remains a persistent challenge. To address this challenge, it is crucial to develop strategies that target the most recurrent crimes, typically property crimes and violence against individuals, and provide appropriate treatment to prevent their reoccurrence. Using a large dataset containing information on inmates with mental health disorders, we developed and executed a counterfactual experiment to determine the effectiveness of treatment in reducing the likelihood of reincarceration within a specific time frame. Based on the results of the experiment, we found that providing appropriate treatment can reduce the likelihood of reincarceration for property crimes and violence against individuals by 30-40% and 20-30% respectively. Additionally, we found that providing treatment can increase the likelihood of inmates finding employment by 40-50% and reducing the likelihood of reincarceration for violent crimes by providing medication specifically for schizophrenia.

A widely adopted semi-supervised learning approach for medical image segmentation uses an interpolation-based mixing technique to combine unbiased model predictions and labeled data for optimization. Conversely, our research proposes a alternative, directly optimizing the model to produce output closest to both the biased predictions and labeled data. This approach was successfully applied to a common network architecture, UNet, resulting in superior performance when tested on a publicly available dataset of brain MRI images. Our results demonstrate that this method yields more accurate image segmentation compared to the standard semi-supervised learning approach. Specifically, our model achieved a mean absolute surface distance of 1.68, outperforming the baseline model with an average distance of 3.51.

To address processing demands for the Large Hadron Collider's upcoming detectors, a scaled-down version of the jet Field-Effect Transistor digital readout system is being developed and tested. This system, comprising eight FENIX modules on a single board, will be assessed for its performance and reliability. A fully functional digital readout system is necessary to efficiently capture data from the LHC's numerous sensors; however, the sheer scale of the data presents a significant challenge. As the LHC's collision rate increases, its sensors must be equipped with faster-than-incremental data processing systems to handle the increased load. With the upcoming LHC runs expected to generate significantly more data, researchers are developing more efficient digital readout systems that can process up to 1.6 terabits of data per second. The jet FEX system, with its data processing speed of approximately 86 gigabits per second, demonstrates the feasibility of these systems. The system's performance was evaluated using beam data at the CERN, and the results showed it could accurately capture the desired data at a rate of 50 megabits per second during 25 nanosecond integration periods. Additionally, the system demonstrated robustness in handling errors, as well as effective use of its four onboard error-correcting modules.

Articulated characters pose a challenge for traditional computer vision approaches due to their complex geometry and dynamic movements. Current deep learning-based methods primarily focus on identifying 3D poses and rendering static objects. In contrast, most everyday applications involve analyzing dynamic scenes, and there is a lack of comprehensive frameworks for tracking the poses and rendering articulated objects. To address this limitation, we introduce Articulated Neural Rendering, a framework that uses a pose-guided decomposition approach to break down input images into pose and object components, allowing for real-time rendering of articulated objects from single images. Our framework encompasses three key components: Pose Estimation, Decomposition, and Reconstruction. We evaluated ART by rendering a range of articulated objects, from 3D shapes to real-world objects, and demonstrated our results against both benchmark datasets and real-world applications, showing that our approach offers a balance of accuracy and efficiency.

We introduce a new method to describe the local atomic structure within a specific distance of a given atom in a solid, using graph neural networks to evaluate the unique atomic environment captured by specific GNN modules. We employ this approach to generate actionable quantities such as effective numbers of atoms, coordination angles, and range of interatomic distances. We evaluate our method by analyzing several model crystal structures and real-world materials, including simple lattices, Clark's rules, Boltzmann dispersion, and actual data from silver and copper. Our approach proves to be robust in predicting these local configuration quantities as a function of temperature.

This paper explores the concept of weak convergence in relation to estimating function parameters, specifically conditions that ensure the consistency of a specific estimator, which arises from a general framework that includes both nonparametric and semiparametric models. Building on established results regarding the consistency of the A_n-estimator, this study identifies conditions that guarantee that the plug-in estimator, based on the estimated parameter, strongly converges to the original parameter value. Corresponding results are established for linear and efficient estimators. Notably, this research demonstrates the utility of the A_n-estimator in the context of linear models, providing conditions for the consistency of the maximum likelihood estimator and a score procedure.

Although the knowledge tracing task has generated significant interest, evaluating deep learning methods for this task remains challenging due to a lack of available evaluation data. This issue is compounded by the need to conduct expensive and time-consuming experiments to compare different models. To address this problem, we propose using a sampling-based evaluation method that is both financially and temporally efficient. This approach involves comparing different models by evaluating them on a limited subset of student data with known learning paths. We demonstrate that this sampling-based evaluation is an unbiased estimator of the true performance and can be scaled up for comparisons across multiple models or evaluation metrics. By utilizing this method, researchers and practitioners can compare multiple deep learning knowledge tracing models in a cost-effective manner, enabling more efficient advancement of this field.

We examine the relationship between being surjective and having a closed graph within the set of smooth functions, in the context of second-order elliptic differential operators. This investigation holds for operators defined on connected, compact manifolds with smooth boundaries. By demonstrating that surjectivity implies a closed graph, we draw upon the work of Taylor to establish this connection. Conversely, we prove that a closed graph yields surjectivity. This result is extended to the context of manifolds that are not necessarily compact through the use of compactifications. Finally, we explore the relationship between being surjective and having a closed graph within the context of higher-order elliptic differential operators.

The veriT proof format was introduced over a decade ago and has experienced significant evolution since its inception. Originally conceived to address the limitations of previous proof standards and exchange formats, veriT has undergone substantial development, reflecting the shifting needs of automated reasoning tools and theorem provers. As a result, veriT now boasts a comprehensive set of features, including support for diverse theorem provers and reasoning engines, as well as an expanded proof content and a refined strategy for proof exploration. This dedicated survey to the veriT proof format provides a detailed exploration of its design principles and operational strategy, as well as a broader perspective on its application scenarios and future directions.

FedBuff is a pioneering example of a private, scalable, and efficient federated learning approach developed to handle massive data sets simultaneously. However, FedBuff is limited to batched updates by leveraging the exponential mechanism to control privacy expenses, limiting its potential to handle non-batched data sets. This paper tackles the challenge of widening FedBuff's applicability to handle unbatched data sets, ensuring clean convergence guarantees through a novel adaptation of the Laplace mechanism in a specific optimization framework. Our proposed method, called Scalable Private FedBuff (SPF), successfully expands the capabilities of FedBuff to handle unbatched data sets, resulting in SPF outperforming FedBuff across various benchmark tasks.

The success of speech recognition systems often relies on extensive data fine-tuning using a large in-domain training set. Yet, certain applications like cross-language transfers or setups with limited in-domain data might benefit from a different approach. Our study focuses on the impact of pre-training speech recognition models on the effectiveness of transfers between languages with varying similarity, including a few with limited data. We found that, despite achieving comparable performance on similar languages through transfer learning, the achievement comes with an increase in data requirements. Furthermore, utilizing the publicly available Librispeech dataset for pre-training enables speech recognition systems to perform cross-language transfers with reduced fine-tuning data on more dissimilar languages, even those with limited data. Comparing our results to previous studies using alternative architectures, we found our method to be competitive.

The emergence of novel node embedding techniques necessitates the development of effective evaluation methods. To address this challenge, we introduce UniEM, a unified framework for node embedding evaluation that compares different algorithms using similar metrics. UniEM's key innovations include: (1) a comprehensive framework for evaluating node embedding algorithms, (2) a set of techniques for experimenting with and visualizing results, and (3) a publicly accessible web interface for user-generated comparisons. To further advance the field, we conduct a comparative study of seven ComPReHensive N ode E mbedding (CHNE) algorithms and provide a comprehensive evaluation of three additional techniques within this field. All implementation details and comparison results are available on the UniEM platform, facilitating transparent and reproducible research.

Within this detection system, we identified a broad structure consisting of $S$-wave contributions and accounted for approximately 4 standard deviations. Recent studies suggest that Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) in a specific mass range could account for all dark matter, and we explore their formation through Haberdashers in this research. Haberdashers are a type of non-linear structure that can lead to PBH creation and form at a scale of $10^{-3}$ times the horizon during the early stages of the universe. We analyze the relationship between the amplitude of a particular primordial power spectrum and the resulting PBH production, and our calculations indicate that in order for PBHs to make up all dark matter, the power spectrum must be within certain limits. These limits put a constraint on the mass of PBHs, and we determine that any structure produced through Haberdashers in a mass range of $10^{8}$ to $10^{11}$ dollars could potentially make up all dark matter.

To accurately measure force in force-controlled actuators like series elastic actuators,  estimate the nonlinear elastic properties and sensor errors,  we develop a novel algorithm.  This method bypasses the conventional use of inverse procedures by instead training a regression model directly on the measurements of force and extension.  We mitigate the impact of measurement noise in sensor data by employing a denoising step before estimating elastic properties.  This algorithm overcomes the limitations of prior methods by handling non-linear elastic behavior, dealing with noisy sensor data, and eliminating the need for inverse procedures.  We evaluate the performance of this algorithm through simulations and physical experiments using a SEA actuator.  The results show that the estimated force matches closely with the actual force, even in the presence of significant extension and nonlinear elastic behavior.  We observe a notable improvement in the algorithm's accuracy when comparing measurements with repeated extensions in the same direction,  by reducing estimation error by an order of magnitude.  Furthermore,  the algorithm excels in estimating force when there are nonlinear elastic behavior patterns,  demonstrating a significant enhancement in performance with a mean absolute error of less than 0.1 N.  Alongside these simulations,  we conduct physical experiments to validate our approach,  achieving a high correlation coefficient of 0.99 and notable improvement in accuracy with a standard deviation of less than 0.1 N.
