The rapid growth of online publications containing valuable security information creates a significant challenge in identifying relevant concepts due to the large amount of unstructured data present. To effectively address this challenge, a method was developed to create a scalable and automated system for extracting security concepts from online blogs and articles. This system utilizes a Bidirectional LSTM neural network to accurately identify relevant phrases and map them to existing security concepts in the MITRE TIPs database. To increase precision, the system incorporates two key optimization techniques: phrase extraction and soft labeling. The optimal combination of features for extraction was determined through a process of feature selection, resulting in a 25% improvement in F1 score. The optimized system demonstrated a remarkable F1 score of 0.788 when evaluating its effectiveness against an independent test set. The system's performance was further showcased by successfully identifying over 300 unique security concepts present in the 700 online blogs used for training.

To address the challenge of detecting magnetic domains within solid materials, research has shifted from conventional mean-field models to statistical physics approaches that account for coexisting opposing magnetic tendencies. In this context, scientists have investigated an opinion formation model with interactions that penalizes discordant opinions, showing it to be a useful representation of magnetization dynamics. This model exhibits behaviors identical to those of the Ising model when there are only two possible opinions, yet its magnetization patterns are more complex in scenarios with multiple opinions. In this study, we adapt the mixed opinion formation model to investigate the dynamics of two competing magnetic domains within an infinite lattice structure. Our findings show the model produces stable waves of opposing magnetization similar to the Ising model, and include a novel feature - a propagating front with fluctuating magnetization. The existence of this front is attributed to the model's ability to support diverse stable states beyond those found in the Ising model. The results provide a theoretical basis for magnet dynamic analysis and may inform detection strategies, although the latter would necessitate empirical validation.

We demonstrate that by incorporating the effects of pollutant accumulation on surface formation through droplet impaction, model predictions align with COVID-19 transmission data. We develop and simplify the model for predicting the time until a critical biofilm layer is reached, making it feasible to estimate the spread of infections within closed environments through numerical simulations.

The convergence of neural networks in solving ill-posed problems and inverse ill-posed problems has long been observed, yet the underlying reason for this success remains unclear. Classical methods tackle such challenges by combining minimal smoothness and prior knowledge through Bayesian frameworks, while alternative approaches use regularization. In this study, we refute the necessity of assuming smoothness or prior knowledge for neural networks to solve inverse ill-posed problems. Instead, we demonstrate that the ability of neural networks to represent any function enables them to naturally overcome ill-posed challenges by default. To support this claim, we provide theoretical evidence of neural network representation capacity and illustrate its application in solving a representative inverse ill-posed problem, the Bernstein basis problem. Our findings are further validated by means of numerical experiments and real-world implementations.

This study examines a specific equality between the symbolic and ordinary power sets of a weighted oriented graph's edge ideal, specifically within a weighted oriented graph's subgraph. The equality holds if and only if a certain local ring's depth matches a related parameter called the symbolic depth. Additionally, this study introduces a parameter called the weak symbolic depth, which is a lower bound for the ordinary and symbolic depths.

Researchers have been using the string theory on a black hole background to study the SU(N) and U(N) partition functions in recent years. A specific lesson learned from these studies is the significance of the Nambu-BCS formula in achieving the exact solution of the model. However, all exact statistical models constructed using this formula have only been confirmed for large N; it is not clear what implications these results have for the behavior of the model when N is finite. In this paper, we use the entanglement entropy of a semi-symmetric phase to demonstrate that the U(N) partition function has unique, detailed structure when N is finite, and that this structure gives rise to the U(N) Nambu-Goto string partition function. Additionally, we show that by applying a specific change of variables, the SU(N) partition function can be made to closely resemble the U(N-1) partition function, allowing us to calculate the SU(N) partition function for any N greater-than or equal to 2.

This paper introduces a novel uniform sampling technique, known as Uniform Batch Sampling (UBS), which enables non-uniform data masking to prevent silent data corruptions in artificial neural networks. By comparing UBS to commonly employed data masking methods, our findings reveal that UBS surpasses both incremental and uniform data masking strategies in robustness against silent data corruptions, with a notable improvement in the latter. We demonstrate that UBS is equally efficient to the incremental method in terms of computational requirements and adaptable to various loss functions, optimization algorithms, and training settings. Additionally, our experiments yield superior outcomes for UBS across diverse evaluation metrics in fair and robust training scenarios for both computer vision and language models.

This paper investigates the complex issue of netting within a economy's payment flows, a problem exacerbated by temporal relationships between transactions. To tackle this challenge, we develop a general framework incorporating several key concepts: payments, transactions, and settlement instructions. Given this framework, our primary objectives involve identifying the optimal ordering of transactions and their corresponding settlement instructions, as well as determining the minimum number of transactions required to achieve settlement. We divide these tasks into two separate problems, solving them through the application of graph algorithms. Specifically, we utilize topological sorting and a variant of the vertex covering problem to achieve our goals. Our approach ensures the elimination of cross-netting vulnerabilities, thereby providing a secure foundation for settlement.

We investigate the Jordanian twist's base case generalizations and prove their equivalence to a single simple Jordanian twist when combined, demonstrating that this mixture doesn't alter the twist's original properties. Additionally, we derive the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula for these combined generalizations.

We introduce a novel approach called maximum entropy maximum marginal likelihood unsupervised learning, which creates a model that adapts both the feature space and model structure to accurately reflect the unknown label distribution. Our method builds upon previous proposals for unsupervised learning, and through experiments in language name tagging with limited data, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to established supervised and unsupervised techniques. Specifically, we find that both the proposed model and our feature selection strategy yield significant improvements over prior methods, achieving an accuracy of 78.5% with just 100 labeled examples in low-resource languages, surpassing the best previous result by 11.3%.

Our findings based on ALICE data reveal trends in particle ratios, specifically $K^./p$ and $p./p$, which exhibit dependence on collision system from p-Pb to Pb-Pb collisions. These trends hold true even as the multiplicity threshold is increased, showing that 0.4 < $K^./p$ < 0.7 and 0.2 < $p./p$ < 1.2 across all studied collisions. Furthermore, we observed an escalating shift in $K^./p$ and $p./p$ ratios with rising charged-particle density, and this escalation grows more pronounced with larger collision systems. In addition, we discovered that 0.4 < $K^./p$ < 0.7 and 0.2 < $p./p$ < 1.2 across all studied collisions, with the dependence on collision system from p-Pb to Pb-Pb. We also found an escalating shift in $K^./p$ and $p./p$ ratios with rising charged-particle density, and this escalation grows more pronounced with larger collision systems. In addition, we discovered that 0.4 < $K^./p$ < 0.7 and 0.2 < $p./p$ < 1.2 across all studied collisions, with the dependence on collision system from p-Pb to Pb-Pb. The growth of large, publicly available datasets has significantly contributed to advancements in natural language processing, but the quality of these datasets is often compromised due to user-generated errors and inconsistencies. This issue is particularly prevalent in the dialogue domain, where the presence of noisy labels can be particularly harmful because they are randomly dispersed, different from both the intended meaning and the actual meaning. This research investigates the consequences of noisy labels on the dialogue state tracking model and demonstrates that they can be remedied with the assistance of correction labels, but this requires vast amounts of annotated data. Furthermore, this work presents a novel method, called diverse decoy selection, that utilizes decoy models with varying levels of performance to evaluate the model's robustness, but does so with significantly reduced computational costs. The proposed diverse decoy selection method is designed to be energy-efficient in that it requires significantly fewer evaluations than previously proposed techniques. The research is conducted on the Allennone dataset and demonstrates that diverse decoy selection can effectively evaluate the model's performance in relation to noisy labels with minimal evaluations, resulting in a significant improvement in the model's performance.

Inspired by the need to understand and improve urban development, researchers are beginning to study cities as living networks. These analyses raise an interesting question about the impact of a city's structure on social phenomena such as riots. To explore this question, we develop a computer model that simulates citizens navigating a city's transportation network, expressing discontent through aggressive behavior, and seeking influence through targeted actions. The model incorporates fundamental urban characteristics found in real cities, such as varying population densities and transportation patterns. As the model is applied to different network configurations, we observe that specific city layouts can either facilitate or hinder the spread of unrest and the emergence of stable social dynamics. Specifically, we found that cities with interconnected neighborhoods and efficient transportation systems are more likely to experience persistent unrest, while those with fragmented districts and better navigation options tend to converge to a stable state more quickly. Our findings suggest that such outcomes depend on the interplay between the city's structural features, its population distribution, and the navigation patterns that emerge as a result of these factors.

Using the PACS photometry from the Herschel Atlas of Galactic OB associations and the Hubble Space Telescope imaging, we have determined the star formation rates and dust grain sizes for 13 OB associations in the galaxy and evaluated the reliability of these results. A comparison of our measurements to previous findings shows good agreement on a majority of points, although there are some discrepancies in the derived star formation rates and dust grain sizes. To assess the accuracy of star formation rate calculations from the Prospector framework, we used a machine learning approach with a subset of 9 associations, and then applied this to the full sample. According to our measurements, the star formation rates in the 13 OB associations in the galaxy range from 0.1 to 10.0 $M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, with a median value of 2.7 $M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$. The dust grain sizes in these associations vary from 1.0 to 2.0 $\mu m$, with a median size of 1.4 $\mu m$. The paper also includes a derived formula for calculating the far-infrared to submillimeter spectral energy distributions of these associations, along with a simplified model for predicting the brightness temperatures of these associations in submillimeter wavelengths.

We provide a unified approach to analyzing the number of sum of squares (SOS) representations and the rank of matrices within a Gram spectrahedron in a sequence of growing dimensions. This involves identifying the maximum possible rank and number of polynomials in an SOS representation at each dimension. We offer specific, universal bounds that guarantee the maximum possible rank or number of SOS representations within the Gram spectrahedron or its subdomain defined by additional non-negative definite matrices. We also establish a broader context for these findings through the lens of matrix perturbation theory and the spectrum of large random matrices. In particular, we show that our derived bounds are nearly achieved on average across all possible matrix choices. To arrive at these results, we developed a novel technique for analyzing the intersection of Hermitian matrix spectra and a critical insight into the structure of non-negative definite matrices that allows us to control the rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron.

To explore neutral long-lived particles resulting from scattering in the ATLAS and CMS experiments, the FASERν experiment will be placed behind CERN's LHC to take advantage of neutrino fluxes produced by the interactions of beam particles and final states with high energy limits. If a neutrino is part of an isolated pair of neutral long-lived particles, its detection in 3000 km of solid rock by the FASERν experiment would impose stringent constraints on its properties. Furthermore, if neither neutrino nor particle is stable, the FASERν experiment can place bounds on the masses and couplings of these particles, which could potentially explain the cosmological dark matter.

We integrate Brzozowski's operator into a symbolic decision procedure for evaluating the containment relationship between regular expressions, enabling the analysis of finite state machines defined by Brzozowski's operator and combining them with star-free expressions via intersection. Although Brzozowski's operator is not definable in traditional anti-unifac expressions, our extension expands the possibilities of symbolic containment analysis by incorporating patterns with recurring cycles, noticeably absent in the existing algorithm by Juhász et al. Although the new algorithm employs a more complex transition function in comparison to the earlier method by Juhász et al., its overall time and memory complexity remain identical to the prior approach. Additionally, our study offers an alternative interpretation of the Starfree Containment Problem by viewing it as checking whether a specific anti-unifac expression contains another, further highlighting the algorithm's versatility.

Deep learning-based Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) models have successfully achieved high accuracy in mapping dynamic environments using camera and inertial sensors. Unlike conventional VIO algorithms that utilize rigid-body motions and feature-based optimization, deep learning-based models leverage raw data to predict pose and map changes. In this study, we evaluate current deep learning VIO models, analyzing their architectures and challenges they pose for real-world applications. Furthermore, we explored integrating an iterative optimization step into these models to improve their accuracy and robustness. Specifically, we examined utilizing the optimal flow criterion as an additional layer in these models. Our experiments demonstrated positive results, showing significant improvements in a challenging real-world scenario. Additionally, we investigated the benefits of incorporating optimization steps in models with different input data frequencies, confirming that such steps are particularly beneficial in scenarios with high inertial sensor updates.

Our investigation focuses on the higher-order Weyl semimetals described by the type-II Weyl Hamiltonian in three-dimensional space. We determine the topological square-root states characterizing these systems through quasi-classical expansions and exact diagrammatic series, and demonstrate that the square-root states originate from the parent Weyl points via smooth parametric variations, thereby establishing a fundamental relationship between them. Additionally, we identify the distinct topological features of the type-II Weyl semimetals, including both the square-root states and surface fermion triply-folded projections, which are directly connected to the type-II Weyl points, and distinguish between them through explicit predictions of transport measurements, specifically the diagonal electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and the triply-folded surface states in the [001] direction, which provides a comprehensive framework for identifying type-II Weyl semimetals.

This study examines various finite element methods on unstructured grids for
solving data completion problems involving analytic functions. Our primary focus
lies on understanding how different elements at the edge level impact the stability
of the discrete problem and, ultimately, the representation of the missing data.
We delve into the specifics of non-conforming and mixed finite elements, as well
as conforming elements with boundary degrees of freedom, analyzing their discrete
equivalence to the optimal recovery operator. Our investigation also extends
to element types such as Nedelec, Raviart-Thomas, and edge rotating Leslie-Schwarz
spaces. In each case, we assess the stability of the associated Schur complement
and provide a representation of the complete data via optimal order approximations.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with the affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, for $n \geq 4$. We establish the generator series and determinant denominator for the Fock space $V_{l_1,\theta}$, determining the central charge as $c_{l_1}=(l_1^2+1)(l_1^2-4)/4$. Furthermore, we identify the irreducible highest weight modules within the vertex operator algebra and determine the fusion algebra, revealing its isomorphism to the $A_3$ simple Lie algebra for the integer values $l_1, l_2 \geq 1$.

This paper presents an innovative method to improve a student model's performance by training it on a subset of data that is considered most relevant to its task of mimicking a robust teacher model. The proposed approach streamlines the training process by limiting the student to specific data points instead of iterating between student and teacher updates. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical and practical evidence. Additionally, the paper showcases how this approach can be applied to a variety of settings, including self-training, knowledge distillation, and an amalgamation of multiple teachers. The proposed method also offers a computationally efficient alternative to standard techniques. The code for the proposed method is openly available, facilitating reproducibility.

Previous research suggested that grid cells, which form a key component of the brain's spatial coding system, generate robust, internally-generated patterns of activity in response to exploration of environmental spaces. In contrast, our findings indicate that grid cells are instead heavily dependent on external visual cues, often becoming desynchronized and losing their periodic patterns when navigated in darkened environments. Furthermore, our results reveal that the cells' activity in response to darkness is distinct from their activity in response to visual cues and other sensory stimuli. In addition, we discovered that grid cells exhibit unique responses to ambient light and visual cues that reflect their sensitivity to the global characteristics of environmental spaces. These conclusions are drawn from a study involving 24 rats, in which we analyzed the neural activity of entorhinal cortex grid cells using extracellular recordings in both brightly lit and darkened environments.

The development of stable and long-term magnetic fields in stars, particularly Kepler stars, has been a subject of research interest lately. This study aims to explore how these stars achieve persistent magnetic field patterns through kinematic dynamo processes. By analyzing pressure scale height and the kinematic dynamo efficiency in stars with varying degrees of rotation, we found that for slowly rotating stars, magnetic cycles could arise due to kinematic dynamo, while rapid rotation would prevent cycle formation. Our model also indicates that magnetic cycles might exist in stars with intermediate rotations. This is consistent with observations of the KY Dra type star. Additionally, we found that magnetic cycles in these stars might be influenced by slow dynamo processes rather than the solar-type alpha-omega dynamo.

We examine a particular type of S4 quartic field extension over a totally real field that has a Galois group isomorphic to a V4 group, focusing on its implications for number theory through the lens of elliptic curves and modular forms. By establishing connections between these two areas, we find that certain V4 quartic extensions can be linked to S4 Hecke eigenforms with a rational coefficient field. Conversely, this allows us to use the geometry of moduli spaces of elliptic curves to create V4 quartic extensions, and conversely. Then, building on earlier work by David, Diamond, and Sasaki, we find that most V4 quartic extensions have a connection to a specific set of elliptic curves with a rational coefficient field. However, for these elliptic curves, having a non-rational rank is equivalent to having a non-rational tau-value that is not an algebraic integer in a specific C4 extension, whose field is a totally real field composed of two S2 extensions, each with a non-rational alpha-value that is not an algebraic integer, over its respective quadratic base field. Consequently, we find that the vast majority of these V4 quartic extensions do not have a non-rational rank. Only those with a C4 Hecke group isomorphic to D4, or those with a Galois group that has a subgroup isomorphic to the V4 group, will have a non-rational rank. Furthermore, focusing on the case where

We examine the time-dependent density-density correlation functions and entropy production in a Luttinger liquid after a quantum quench, considering both temperature change and change in interaction strength. By modifying the interaction strength and temperature in specific ways, we demonstrate that the total entropy generation equals the difference in entropy for the initial and final equilibrium states, as predicted by the equilibrium quench theorem. Furthermore, we observe that the change in temperature during the quench is directly proportional to the average energy density, in alignment with previous findings. Additionally, we note that the entropy generation during the quench can be understood through the change in temperature and the shift in the interaction strength. Specifically, the change in entropy is the sum of the entropy change due to the temperature change and the change in entropy due to the change in interaction strength.

We investigate the long-term behavior of a system interacting with an environment, focusing on how components of the system time-evolve relative to each other. By developing a new measure of time-twirling in both unitary and non-unitary dynamics, we show that it directly correlates with the distinguishability time. Specifically, we find that the time-twirling of the total system state converges to a steady-state that reflects the relative times of system components, and this occurs by the same time-scale as distinguishability. Additionally, we identify that this time-twirling pattern is unique and can be used to reconstruct the time-twirling of the initial system state. As a result, we are able to distinguish system components based on their time-twirling and provide an upper bound on the time-twirling of the system state. This ability to identify time-twirling arises from the unitary nature of the system-environment interaction and does not rely on the system being isolated. Instead, it relies on the system's interaction with its environment, and thus it provides an environmentally-driven perspective on time-twirling.

We demonstrate that within the unit cube of n dimensions, there exists a regular simplex in need of fewer than n^2 interpolation nodes to fully capture its essence, provided that the number of nodes exceeds n. Additionally, we show this minimum number of nodes is the best possible for both dimensions two and three. Our proof involves constructing a set of interpolation nodes that defines a nondegenerate simplex within the unit cube of any dimension greater than six.

The carrier concentration in etched silicon, a crucial parameter for high-energy physics, can be influenced by different factors including the type of etching process. Two common methods, buffer oxide etching and silicon etching, may result in varying carrier concentrations due to the etching agents used. Our research compares these two approaches by measuring the carrier concentration in both types of etched silicon, revealing a higher concentration in etched silicon than in oxide etched silicon. To mitigate this difference, a method of compensatory doping was developed to align the carrier concentrations in both types of etched silicon. Our findings show that with compensatory doping, the difference in carrier concentration can be minimized to less than 100 fc/100, meeting the requirements for the ATLAS ITK prototype.

This study combines the principles of cdh descent and Milnor excision with the mutated $\mathrm{KH}^*(X)$ formula initially presented by Jannicam Jacobs in his work. As a result, we derive a more general formula for $\mathrm{KH}^*(X)$ that incorporates cdh descent and Milnor excision, and from this, we obtain $\mathrm{KH}^*(X)$ formulas for a broader category of quasicompact, quasiclosed schemes over a perfect field of characteristic zero. Our investigation into twisted homotopy K-theory leads to the introduction of a mutation of twisted motivic homotopy K-theory, which we denote as $\mathrm{KH}^*_s(X)$. We establish that this mutated theory is equivalent to cdh-invariant twisted homotopy K-theory, and that it preserves the properties of motivic cohomology. We also establish the representability of $\mathrm{KH}^*_s(X)$ through rational motivic cohomology sheaves, and we provide the structure of these sheaves. Finally, we prove that for any scheme of dimension at most one, $\mathrm{KH}^*_s(X)$ is isomorphic to twisted homotopy K-theory calculated using the map $X\to \mathrm{Spec}(k)$.

The evolution of an exoplanet's atmosphere may be shaped by a recurring cycle between its interior and exterior layers. This cycle could potentially account for the stable, habitable conditions observed on planets like Kepler-452b. To further understand this potential cycle, we've developed a simplified model that incorporates both radiative cooling at the surface and heat generation within the planet. By analyzing this model, we find that the cycle indeed exists and is governed by a constant ratio of heat generation to cooling rates. This ratio ultimately determines the planet's overall temperature. It's interesting to note that this temperature is in fact independent of the heat generation constant and cooling rate. This means that even if the planet's interior or atmospheric conditions change, the surface temperature will remain the same, achieving a thermodynamic equilibrium. This concept may be applied to planets like Kepler-452b, where the estimated heat generation and cooling rates suggest a surface temperature compatible with life as we know it.

A computational study is carried out on the methylation of 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PDO) and 1,3-propanediol (1,3-PDO) using density functional theory with effective core pseudopotentials. Calculations of reaction paths and energy barriers are performed in gas and aqueous phases. It is found that 1,2-PDO forms a cyclic structure, making it less accessible to methylation, whereas 1,3-PDO can be easily methylated. In aqueous solution, both isomers exhibit an equilibrium between cyclic and open structures, favoring the latter, and it is this structure that methylation targets. As a result, 1,3-PDO is more readily converted to its methylated counterpart than 1,2-PDO. These findings are consistent with earlier experimental observations highlighting 1,3-PDO's greater reactivity in comparison to 1,2-PDO.

Deep quantum circuits are highly expressive but their complexity limits them, whereas tensor networks balance representational power with circuit depth. Our work shows that deep quantum circuits contain a significant portion that can be decomposed into shallow circuits combined with local unitary operations. We further find that many tensor networks are structurally equivalent to deep circuits holding a specific symmetry, leveraging this to create a universal quantum circuit-to-tensor-network mapping. Consequently, our approach enables the application of classical minimization techniques to optimize tensor network parameters. Our findings specifically benefit time-evolving variational quantum circuits and multilayer tensor network architectures.

Cancer research utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to distinguish between tumor and normal tissue representations, which have shown significant potential. However, the transparency of these complex models is a major concern for healthcare professionals who need to integrate them into their practice. Furthermore, the predictive models are often developed without being fully interpreted and understood, which raises questions about their reliability. Although some recent studies have explored the interpretability of GNNs in cancer analysis, they face significant challenges due to the inherent complexity of the models and the sensitivity of their outputs. In our research, we address the issue of interpretability by providing an intuitive visualization of the classification process and the underlying decision-making mechanisms of the GNN model. In order to achieve this, we apply a technique called Feature Importance Explanation (FIE) to each node in the graph, which allows us to assign an importance score to each feature based on its impact on the classification outcome. By applying FIE, we can offer the healthcare professionals a clear understanding of the classification process and provide them with actionable insights that can be utilized in their daily work, ultimately facilitating the integration of these complex models into the healthcare sector.

This work extends the linear Hawkes process to a nonlinear model that
accounts for complex interactions within a network of multiple event streams.
We apply the Ragsdale-Miller estimation method for the nonlinear Hawkes
process, introducing a new decay function that maintains differentiability
for the partial likelihood optimization. We further develop a nonparametric
estimation approach for the nonlinear Hawkes process, suggesting a general
framework that includes previous studies. Simulation results demonstrate the
advantages of our specific linear estimator, while theoretical orthogonality
proof for the estimation errors appears in the supplemental materials. We
analyze the Portland pedestrian traffic data, revealing a linear relationship
between male and female traffic flows, but the Hawkes process is shown to
notfully capture interaction effects. Furthermore, our results identify notable
features in the estimated decay functions and the estimated Hawkes process
spectral densities.

We've introduced an open-source, flexible implementation of the fast multipole method (FMM) for computing near-field interactions in simulations of astrophysical systems, primarily focusing on gravitational interactions. By incorporating multiple hierarchy options and boundary checking techniques within the FMM framework, our implementation offers significant performance enhancements, with certain applications reaching up to 21 times faster execution times compared to existing methods. These optimizations, combined with our choice of efficient data structures and lightweight memory usage, are key contributors to these performance gains. Additionally, we've found that our FMM implementation produces accurate results, consistent with expectations for $O(N)$ FMM algorithms, and is particularly suited for processing large datasets in the context of astrophysical simulations.

Cross-domain adaptation is a key technique in medical image segmentation, enabling the application of accurate models across different anatomical regions without needing separate models for each domain. However, existing methods primarily focus on adapting between domains that have similar image characteristics and aren't sufficiently robust to tackle the challenge of adapting across significantly different anatomical domains, such as adapting a brain segmentation model for use in abdominal imaging. To tackle this more complex challenge, we propose a contrastive semi-supervised learning approach for Cross-Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that incorporates a contrastive loss function to learn a more domain-invariant representation. By semi-synchronously applying the contrastive loss function on both target and source domains during training, we can reduce the gap between these domains and adapt across more anatomically distant domains. Our CS-CADA approach was evaluated on the challenging task of adapting brain segmentation models for use in abdominal imaging, using the STENTOR dataset. Our results show that CS-CADA achieves highly accurate adaptations, with a 38% increase in Dice score compared to existing methods.

To comprehend 4D supersymmetric gravity, we suggest transforming it into a non-gravitational model, which would involve a change of variables and a non-standard procedure for constrained systems. This transformation might provide the necessary basis for a proper analysis of the symmetry in this system, potentially allowing us to determine the representative fields and simplify the algebra of constraints. Using this approach, we demonstrate the equivalence between the original and transformed theories, and the simplicity of the symmetry in the new formulation. Additionally, we discuss the implications of using this non-gravitational description for calculating physical observables in 4D supersymmetric gravity, and consider the possibility of applying this method to other complex systems, such as gravity coupled to an antisymmetric tensor field, for which the algebra of constraints is difficult to solve analytically.

A key component for converting circularly polarized microwaves to linearly polarized microwaves is the plasma waveplate, and its effectiveness depends on achieving a specific thickness. This study explores the minimum required thickness as a function of plasma electron density, magnetic field strength, and frequency. The results show that the optimal thickness should be greater than a specific value, determined by the product of the plasma electron density and the square of the electron gyroradius, and should also be in the range of one to two times the plasma layer thickness. Notably, a threshold electron density exists below which the plasma waveplate fails to function. Additionally, the optimal thickness is influenced by the strong field limit and the harmonic number of the microwave, and can be both smaller and larger than the optimal thickness, respectively.

We investigate how the Standard Model can be expanded with a two-Higgs doublet model, specifically focusing on the scenario where one Higgs doublet contributes to an electric dipole moment, whereas the other remains neutral. By assessing the constraints imposed by experimental data and theoretical stability, we find that we can anticipate a significant contribution to the tau electric dipole moment, with a predicted value in the range of $10^{-18}$ degrees. Additionally, we explore the possibility of this model being consistent with the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry and find that it may not efficiently produce the desired effect unless it includes heavy neutrino modes. Furthermore, we investigate the potential for this model to be probed at current and upcoming experiments, including those for Higgs boson interactions and electric dipole moments.

Rank metric codes can be utilized in storage devices that suffer from both data corruption and erasures. We provide the fundamental framework for decoding these codes, focusing on minimum rank per node and all-or-nothing failures. We establish the overall failure pattern tolerance of these codes, with specific decoding efficiency examined for certain failure patterns. Moreover, we investigate the applicability of these codes at different data utilization rates and find that they can correct errors for rates below 1/2 but not above 1/2.

The structure of conformal block operators in two-dimensional conformal field theory can be examined through the lens of AdS$_3$ geometry, specifically by considering the geodesic operator framework in this context. It has been found that these conformal block representations can be modified to account for conserved current blocks in a precise manner. By taking a limit, the geodesic operator representations can be shown to be equivalent to their counterparts in AdS$_2$ geometry. Furthermore, this equivalence enables a direct computation of Casimir operators acting on two-dimensional conformal blocks. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator form can be utilized to derive the coefficient $c$ in Boehringer's formula for the dual density operator in tensored systems. A similar calculation applies to the entanglement density operator.

We employed Gaussian processes and deep convolutional neural networks to analyze their effectiveness in reconstructing gravitational lensing mappings using weak-lensing data, and found that the neural networks achieved comparable results to traditional estimators with a 30% reduction in noise. Analyzing the impact of pixel migration in shear estimates revealed that neural networks are more resilient, and we discovered that using a range of neural network hyperparameters does not significantly impact results. Additionally, we found that using a range of traditional estimators does have a significant impact on results.

In 2008, David Eisenbud published a study that built upon the work of Gelfand and MacPherson, exploring the properties of combinatorial differential manifolds through the lens of their rational singularities. This research, in turn, paved the way for the development of new techniques in computing the Chow and Puiseux voltages of these manifolds. This paper aims to supplement Eisenbud's findings, with a particular focus on analyzing the Puiseux voltages of combinatorial differential manifolds in a more general context.

We performed high-resolution spectroscopy of the young stellar system N159F2,
within which the stellar wind and supersonic outflows were generated by
analyzing the He II $\lambda{1640}$ line in spectra obtained with VLT/UVES.
Our observations from 2019 to 2020 encompassed the formation of multiple
transient sources within this region, including SN~2020jfo, which became a gamma-ray
burst GBM20uxf associated with a massive star. Our data show how the spectral
line varied over time and allowed for the identification of several components,
including narrow absorption lines in the system and broader lines in the gas within
the stellar wind. The broad lines in the wind gas showed a velocity structure that
mirrors the shape of the photospheric velocity curve, and they also exhibited a
central narrow absorption line that may indicate the presence of a small, compact
density within the stellar wind. The spectral line profiles also indicated significant
absorption variations over time, which may be attributed to the motion of broad
absorption lines across the line of sight as well as changes in the column densities
of narrow lines associated with different radial components of the wind. Our analysis
yielded a detailed picture of the wind structure in N159F2, which is characterized
by numerous narrow absorption lines originating from various radial components and
encompassing a broad absorption line with a velocity full width of approximately
230 km/s.

A lobster-eye optics system employs a unique cross-like image to determine the position of its internal structure and orient its optical axis. We investigate an alternative method of analyzing this cross-like image by dividing it into four sections and calculating the rotation angle in the azimuthal plane. We examine the effect of using this rotation angle on our ability to locate the optics structure and orient the optical axis. We find that using the azimuthal rotation angle in this way significantly improves our accuracy in locating the structure and orienting the optical axis, even when only using one image. Additionally, we find that using this method allows us to use information from multiple images to further refine our accuracy.

We employ a level set formulation to investigate solutions to second order fully nonlinear partial differential equations, specifically equations of the form $F(x,u,Dp DP^2u)=0$. Our approach enables us to examine the higher order properties of solutions by leveraging the level set method's ability to capture geometric information and ensure the propagation of highest order features. Building on previous work, we develop an approach to ensure that solutions maintain the highest possible order of smoothness, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a broad class of fully nonlinear equations, including those involving degenerate operators.

Using the MIT-HU/CfA $N$-body simulation at different levels of initial perturbations, we compare the predictive abilities of halo models constructed from density and/or velocity profiles.  In simulations with $\sigma_8 = 0.94$, which aligns with current observations, we find that using density-only information reduces the accuracy of halo mass predictions, with a median offset of $+0.11$ $\log_{10} M_\odot$ when compared to predictions derived from density and velocity profiles.  However, in simulations with more significant perturbations, $\sigma_8 = 0.80$, we find that velocity profiles become increasingly important, and using density-only information results in a significant offset of $+0.24$ $\log_{10} M_\odot$.  We demonstrate that this sensitivity to velocity profiles is attributed to deviations of the $\Lambda$CDM model from its asymptotic predictions, specifically the breakdown of halo clusters into transient structures in regions with high amplitude perturbations.  Given the accuracy requirements for current and forthcoming galaxy surveys, which demand halo mass predictions with an offset of $0.10$ $\log_{10} M_\odot$ or lesser, we recommend utilizing halo models constructed from density and velocity profiles for all scenarios, regardless of the amplitude of initial perturbations.

This study introduces a semi-supervised Convolutional Neural Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method for automatic piano transcription. CNMF combines the advantages of low-rank factorization techniques and supervised deep learning methods, leveraging both local pattern recognition and long-distance structure information, as well as limited labeled data and vast unlabeled data. The proposed semi-supervised CNMF (ssCNMF) method iteratively refines a low-rank representation of piano spectra using both labeled and unlabeled data, with a focus on minimizing errors in labeled samples and maintaining the factorization's structural integrity across unlabeled data. The development of ssCNMF leads to significant improvements in piano transcription accuracy, with performance exceeding that of leading low-rank factorization methods and surpassing that of supervised deep learning approaches even with limited training data.

This research introduces a novel approach to assigning mass and angular momentum to individual fluid components within stars that rotate. Unlike conventional methods, this approach bypasses the utilization of corotational coordinates and instead directly specifies mass and angular momentum through a set of differential equations that define the trajectories of these fluid elements across space and time. A computational framework is created to solve these equations by leveraging an explicit second-order precise predictor-corrector method, thereby enabling simulations of rotating stars with intricate patterns of matter flow. Schemes such as the artificial viscosity method and the successive over-relaxation method are incorporated to handle potential numerical oscillations and alignment errors. A key aspect of this research involves conducting simulations of barotropic stars undergoing frame-dumping events and presenting the results in a manner compatible with post-Newtonian expansions.

Using a limited amount of selectively labeled data efficiently is crucial for ongoing learning and data collection. The cost of obtaining accurate annotations is high, but they are necessary to improve models and expand the scope of data used for training. A method was developed to determine the most effective way to label new data based on its potential impact on future model performance. This approach takes into account the diversity of data and ensures that the most useful examples are identified and targeted for annotation. Experimental results show that this method adds the fewest possible labels while achieving the greatest improvement in model performance, and it can handle large datasets by using a random sampling approach. The method was tested on supervised online learning tasks, including text classification and sentiment analysis, and it led to significant reductions in the number of labels needed, with an average decrease of 50% or more, depending on the dataset.

The convergence of gravitational and electromagnetic observation capabilities in the study of neutron star mergers has significantly boosted the science from these events. The union of gravitational waves and multi-spectral electromagnetic radiation provides valuable insights into the merger process, its remnants, and the environmental conditions. Furthermore, the ability to observe neutron star mergers using both gravitational waves and neutrinos offers a holistic understanding of these events. The simultaneous use of these observation methods has already yielded significant insights into neutron star mergers and is expected to produce more informative results in the future, particularly with the advancement of wide-band gravitational wave detectors and improved electromagnetic telescope arrays.

The understanding of social determinants of health can be expanded by incorporating contextual, location-based information, but this data is frequently gathered through informal means such as clinical notes that need to be interpreted manually.  To address this challenge, we propose a method to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from structured electronic health records and geographic data.  By developing a customized knowledge base that maps concepts from the SDoH to those in the UMLS, we employed string and machine learning-based techniques to identify and extract information from notes that was not previously encoded in the health records.  With this approach, we were able to identify and extract nearly 20% more information about the SDoH from notes that was not previously encoded in the health records.  Furthermore, our results showed that our approach could accurately identify around 90% of newly extracted information with a high confidence level.  This method has been successfully applied to analyze around 300,000 notes from around 200,000 unique patients and around 50,000 individuals with various conditions, and it is readily available for use in the health industry via an API.

We have examined the movement of a swimmer that alternates between two fixed locations under various switching rates and discovered that its transportation costs are minimized at a specific rate that is proportional to its overall speed. This optimal rate varies depending on the swimmer's speed and switching facility and is expressed in terms of these factors. Furthermore, we found that when the switching rate is higher than this optimal rate, the cost increases in a way that reflects the value of patience in waiting for a suitable opportunity to swim.

Our analysis of an informal network of artists in Montreal reveals how the COVID-19 pandemic's sudden and intense measures affected urban encounters and community resilience in the city over the course of three decades, from 1990 to 2021. We found substantial variations in network connectivity, ranging from high mobility during the pandemic to the extreme isolation of the great lockdown, and eventually returned to pre-pandemic levels of connectivity. We examined the diversity of urban encounters by studying travel patterns within the network and found them to be more localized and fragmented during the pandemic, but eventually returned to pre-pandemic levels of diversity. We found evidence of a surge in community resilience marked by a rise in exclusive relationships and a shift towards more localized and interconnected groups, but this surge was short-lived and mostly occurred within the first two years of the pandemic. In the long term, we observed a decline in community resilience, with a shift towards more isolated and dispersed connections, and a rise in connections with travel patterns that no longer relied on daily urban encounters. These changes indicate a potential shift towards a new normal, but we cannot rule out the possibility that things might return to normal once the pandemic's lasting effects on people's behaviors subside.

The massive young stellar object DL Cha is surrounded by a disc that undergoes significant migration patterns. Researchers have proposed that the inner disc's instability and unusual dynamics can be attributed to the presence of two prominent dust rings. A computer simulation demonstrates that, when these migrating targets are included, the inner disc displays greater stability and more consistent orbital patterns. However, when the dust rings migrate innerwards, the inner disc becomes unstable, resulting in the formation of unstable orbital patterns and eventually, the creation of dust rings similar to those observed around DL Cha.

Building upon established theories, this paper defines a scattering matrix and an associated algebra for a specific class of operators that satisfies asymptotic compatibility. Key properties, including the structure of the algebra and scattering matrix, are established through careful analysis. Additionally, this paper explores a complementary algebra and determines the relationship between these algebras and the scattering matrix. Key properties, including the structure of the algebra and matrix, are established through careful analysis. Furthermore, this paper explores a complementary algebra and determines the relationship between these algebras and the scattering matrix.

As 5G cellular towers spring up, concerns about their safety are surfacing, with some advocating for a more thorough assessment of the elevated 5G exposure levels. To address this issue, researchers reviewed existing studies on exposure levels from 5G and 4G infrastructure, also recalculating predicted exposure levels based on current measurements, with a focus on locations within EU countries. The analysis revealed that, when considering building attenuation, the 5G exposure levels significantly exceed those of 4G, with the difference being particularly pronounced in areas near basestations. However, when taking into account the buffering effect of outdoor environmental factors, the levels generally dropped below those of 4G. The findings suggest that a more detailed assessment of the elevated 5G exposure levels is indeed warranted, with implications for revised exposure limit policies.

This study introduces a novel approach to analyzing complex water waves, based on a parametric representation of the free surface. A specific transformation of the coordinates leads to a simplified form of the governing equations, making them more manageable than previously anticipated. Although the method still yields moderately difficult to solve boundary value problems, it allows for the efficient application of numerical methods to solve the resulting equations. Specifically, the article demonstrates how the method can be utilized with a Chebyshev spectral collocation technique to accurately solve the water wave problem. The method proves particularly effective in recovering the surface elevation from the wave envelope and even demonstrates some interesting properties when applied to fundamental waves and solitons.

The surface layer theorem, initially applicable to differential forms in finite-dimensional spaces, has been expanded to account for locally convex spaces. This expansion takes into consideration the convex sets characterized by local absolute convexity properties. A new theorem regarding the surface layer theorem is presented, which enables the localization of differential forms expressed in a finite-dimensional form within these sets.

This paper presents a novel control system with multiple layers for mobile platforms that use sonar sensors to navigate in their environment. We demonstrate how the layer system's collaborative effort expands the navigation capabilities of these platforms by enabling them to overcome obstacles and navigate through various surroundings, ultimately resulting in enhanced performance. We also provide a detailed analysis of the layer system's design and functionality, along with the advantages it offers. Additionally, we present a practical application of the layer system, where it is implemented on a mobile robot using the MATLAB Simulink tool.

The impact of artificial intelligence has spread across various sectors with language models, transforming how information is processed, yet they've also given rise to new challenges like the spread of fake news. This issue's complexity lies in its inherent connection to social networks, cultures, and governments, making it crucial to investigate its solutions globally. In this research, we're exploring the question of whether and how much context is essential for identifying fake news. We've developed and tested two types of models, one with context and the other without, using a multilingual dataset, and our results show that the model with context performs better and the importance of context varies depending on the language used. These findings suggest that context is crucial in detecting fake news, especially for languages with limited resources.

We have developed a comprehensive linearized theory that applies to elastic systems possessing rotational symmetry and a curved geometry. This mathematical framework simplifies the thermodynamic analysis, allowing us to examine how the elastic response is affected by the degree of curvature. Notably, we observe that increasing curvature results in hysteresis and a more complex entropy change. This phenomenon is further explored using a simple elastic model with a circular cross-section, where we investigate how curvature affects the entropy and hysteresis by analyzing the stress-strain relationship. Additionally, we propose a new metric that quantifies the difference in entropy between expanding and contracting elastic systems.

Our proposed suboptimal policy reduces complex subproblems to linear equations, simplifying order selection computations. This method limits the average computational burden per user to a constant, while ensuring faster overall decoding process.

We introduce a novel method to solve a rotationally invariant L1-PCA model, which is based on an alternative two-block representation. This method involves an indicator matrix and a covariance matrix, constrained by the condition that the row sums of the former equal zero. Due to the lack of specific algorithms for this model, we developed a block-coordinating algorithm to solve the two-block representation. This algorithm consists of two coordinate descent methods: an iterative thresholding method for the indicator matrix and a least-squares method for the covariance matrix. Moreover, we established the convergence rate of our algorithm and its average time complexity. Through simulated data and real applications, we evaluated the performance of this algorithm, comparing it to an IPFP-coordinating algorithm that uses an interior point method for the covariance matrix.

Although data annotation holds great potential for machine learning, ensuring the quality of a large annotation dataset remains a significant challenge. A key issue lies in verifying the consistency of annotations, particularly for large-scale datasets with numerous instances. This work proposes a novel approach to achieve this goal by leveraging the paraphrasing technique for validation. Specifically, we suggest using paraphrasing tasks to generate alternative annotations for the same instance, with the aim of validating the original annotations. By comparing the generated alternatives to existing annotations, we can determine the consistency of those annotations. Moreover, we demonstrate that a method based on contrastive learning effectively identifies inconsistent annotations. To further enhance the validation process, we propose incorporating feedback from human annotators to fine-tune the model's performance. Ultimately, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach by validating a large annotation dataset of semantic labeling tasks.

The concept of half-positional winning conditions in two-player games was initially explored and a notable property confirmed about their union with prefix-independent conditions. This study delves deeper, questioning whether the combination of all such conditions would yield a positional winner set able to accommodate all instances of the original games. Our findings establish that such a positional winner set does exist, providing a specific pattern as a substitute for deriving it, and also proving that any instance of a game with a half-positional condition can be matched by an instance of a game with a positionally determinate condition. Additionally, a non-half-positional condition is identified that results from combining two half-positional conditions, thereby necessitating the restriction to prefix-independent conditions for maximal coverage.

Our X-ray and optical investigations into the asynchronous polar V1213 Horologii and the rare earth polar V2115 Ophiuchi have revealed distinct insights. Analyzing 9 years of X-ray data from the Telescopes and Instrument Team Catalogue, we discovered that V1213 Horologii exhibits a higher X-ray persistence duration than the asynchronous polar V2115 Ophiuchi. Furthermore, V1213 Horologii displays X-ray spectra characteristic of a hotter neutron star tail, similar to those found in standard polars, whereas V2115 Ophiuchi has the most temperature gradient reported for a polar's X-ray spectrum. This difference in X-ray spectra may be attributed to V2115 Ophiuchi's higher mass transfer rate that fills its neutron star and accretion column, possibly leading to more efficient release of its stored heat during X-ray flares.

To tackle Fluid-Structure-Interaction (FSI) challenges, a broken-down method has gained popularity, which involves solving the fluid and solid components separately using different techniques. Despite this, integrating the results from both parts with accuracy remains a significant issue. The typical procedure involves transferring the structural values to the fluid through a boundary that changes over time, often with undesirable consequences like excessive oscillations and loss of energy. To address this, a novel approach is proposed, which involves breaking down the time steps into smaller parts and using different boundary conditions for each. Furthermore, to enhance stability, a gradual transition method is introduced. The proposed approach is tested on a classic beam in fluid scenario, which showcases significant improvements in both stability and energy preservation.

Local metric maps in robotics are typically limited to navigating within a confined space, but such approaches can be combined with hierarchical structures like topological maps to expand navigation capabilities to larger areas. Despite advances in mapping technologies like lidar and camera-based sensing, building accurate maps from noisy sensor data remains a significant challenge. We present a new type of hierarchical map called HiTMap, created by processing lidar and GPS data and applying a novel clustering technique, but what makes HiTMap unique is its localized construction method. Most mapping approaches construct a grid or set of points from sensor data, but HiTMap's nodes are positioned based on their connectivity, size, and shape, making it a truly graph-based representation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap by navigating a mobile robot through several loops at the IROS 2018 competition in Italy using the MTMC benchmark, achieving a high ranking with low loss and no spikes.

We implemented a multi-task convolutional neural network and a contrasting
schedule for training data, which significantly boosted the detection of
abusive language in tweets. With the system being trained on a diverse range of
datasets, it achieved a macro F1 score of 0.9075, an accuracy of 0.9472,
precision of 0.8843, and F1 score of 0.8843 for classifying hate speech.

Using atomic interferometry, it is suggested that local magnetic fields can be detected with extraordinary sensitivity at the $10^{-18}$ tesla level. This extremely refined detection capability can potentially allow for the identification of non-local magnetic fields generated by dark matter. To achieve this, an atomic clock is manipulated through a path that intersects a target location where the magnetic field needs to be measured. The result is obtained by analyzing the shift in frequency of the atomic clock due to differential phase shifts as atoms pass through two identically designed interferometry setups, one with their internal spins aligned with the magnetic field and the other against it. This method can allow for the detection of local magnetic fields without being hindered by interactions with dark matter.

Our calculations show that incorporating a ferromagnetic layer with a negative MCE into a heterostructure, joined with a freestanding FeMoP layer exhibiting positive MCE, enables independent control over the thermal expansion in spin-up and spin-down states. Using interlayer coupling, we can tune the electron occupation to align with spin-up or spin-down states, thereby controlling the MCE in these layers. Consequently, we can achieve non-lattice-driven magnetic cooling in the FeMoP layer while simultaneously heating the ferromagnetic layer, thus obtaining a net magnetic cooling in the heterostructure. The heat current direction can also be reversed by modifying the electron occupation, resulting in heating in the FeMoP layer and cooling in the ferromagnetic layer. This heterostructure concept offers possibilities for MCE technology applications.

The traditional local model fails to accurately depict light behavior within small gaps, typically narrower than one wavelength. In contrast, the proposed effective gap width approach successfully predicts light propagation even in minuscule gaps, outperforming local models in this regard. Additionally, this new method provides a more sustainable and practical framework for calculating energy losses in complex systems than alternative methods, which are often confined to specific contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using the effective gap width approach, model periodic cavities with arbitrary shapes and sizes, and show that it aligns with intuitive descriptions of light behavior. Lastly, we apply this model to enhance the quasi-periodic grating effect in a specific photonic device design.

The calculus of constructions was a highly influential construct in multiple areas including programming languages and type theory. Its innovative use of a type-level substitution function addressed various concerns, ultimately contributing to the development of multiple programming languages and theories. This project delves into a detailed examination of the calculus of constructions, incorporating both formal and informal descriptions of its core concepts and mechanisms. Additionally, it provides an in-depth analysis of how the calculus's constructs have been implemented in real-world programming languages and how it has influenced various aspects of programming and type theory.

The development of new technologies such as spintronics and superconducting electronics relies heavily on the precise analysis of second-order electronic response functions. Entanglement concepts like the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix method can help analyze these response functions. This article discusses how these methods for quantifying entanglement can be adapted to examine interacting systems in steady-state and oscillatory conditions. It also explores the utility of these entanglement measures in investigating quantum electronics using an example based on the Drude model with a superconducting gap.

In the context of mixture models, where components correspond to unknown probability densities, it's commonly possible to recover the admixture weights explicitly. Conversely, if we place a Dirichlet process prior on these densities, the resulting mixture model typically yields non-identifiable admixture weights. This work contradicts the widely-held assumption that such models necessarily suffer from this limitation. By developing a general strategy for retrieving the identifiable admixture weights, we demonstrate that they can indeed be recovered in this case. Our approach is then applied to a DP-based mixture model featuring exponential kernel, for which we derive a closed-form expression for the desired admixture weights. Furthermore, we establish the consistency of our proposed weight estimation method.

An analysis of two-loop corrections to the anomalous dimensions of certain four-tweak operators within N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence, has been performed. Specifically, calculations were carried out to determine the anomalous dimensions, allowing for the confirmation or rejection of specific conjectures regarding the structure of the dilatation operator. Furthermore, the accuracy of a proposed two-loop formula for the anomalous dimensions in question was verified for all relevant orders.

In order to overcome the limitations of traditional GPU memory allocators, which lack recursion and dynamic linking capabilities, DynaSOAr was developed. This concurrent, lock-free allocator enables dynamic loading of binary codes and recursion within GPU applications. By dynamically managing memory blocks and efficiently handling free lists, DynaSOAr executes tasks in parallel while minimizing fragmentation and boosting performance. Compared to standard GPU allocators, DynaSOAr demonstrates superior performance, with speeds 5-30 times faster, and exhibits robust results in terms of memory fragmentation. Additionally, DynaSOAr's ability to handle recursive functions and dynamic linking opens up new possibilities for complex GPU applications, and its streamlined design makes it an ideal base for more advanced allocators.

This research paper investigates the boundedness of various operators, including the maximal operator, singular integral operators, and fractional maximal operators, on a specific space called generalized mixed Morrey spaces. The study also examines the compactness of these operators within the same space. Additionally, the paper identifies the optimal mixed Morrey norms that guarantee the boundedness of these operators. Furthermore, a specific operator called the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator is found to be bounded on a particular subset of generalized mixed Morrey spaces, surpassing the limitations imposed by the Morrey inequality.

We studied Ytterbium surface states near the Kondo breakdown, using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, with strong spin-orbit coupling on a Germanium surface that has a lattice structure similar to that of Ytterbium. Our research showed that small magnetic adatoms or pairs of magnetic adatoms cause significant changes in Ytterbium surface states, especially in the vicinity of their Kondo breakdown point, where a peak should exist. However, only altering the chemical potential is enough to move this peak out of this Ytterbium spectrum range. Furthermore, this peak can reappear with increased spin-orbit coupling, and we found that this coupling makes the Ytterbium surface states more fragile and have a more distinct flat-band character. Our research also revealed that a pair of magnetic adatoms has a more substantial effect on these Ytterbium surface states, especially when they form a Kondo cluster, and that this influence extends over a larger area than that of a single adatom.

Recently, Implicit Masking has gained popularity due to its capability to create complex mask shapes without relying on grid-based operations. However, generating high-resolution masks from lower-resolution masks remains a challenge for current implicit masking approaches. To tackle this problem, we propose FourierMask, a novel implicit masking model that uses Fourier series to represent implicit functions and evaluates the method's effectiveness for high-resolution mask generation from downsampled masks. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements, around 10%, in accuracy compared to existing implicit masking solutions, as well as around 30%, in accuracy when using Fourier series alone, without the need for post-processing. Furthermore, FourierMask exhibits the ability to create more accurate boundary definitions, outperforming competitors by around 20%, as measured by the boundary metric, IoU boundary.

This study focuses on the fundamental issue of whether there are entire, bounded minimal disks in three-dimensional space that correspond to a given, simply connected submanifold with a specific pinched curvature condition. Previously, this concern had been addressed for submanifolds with certain specific properties. This research expands those findings by establishing the existence of these minimal disks for a broader category of submanifolds: those with certain mild properties and a pinch ratio close enough to 1. To achieve this, new interpolation methods are introduced, allowing for the construction of a more general class of submanifolds with a pinch ratio even closer to 1. Additionally, this research demonstrates that there are entire, bounded minimal disks in three-dimensional space that correspond to a given, closed submanifold with a pinch ratio arbitrarily close to 1, and a certain condition is met regarding its fundamental volume and surface volume.

The method we propose is suitable for analyzing aerial images, specifically for detecting and classifying thickly populated areas within cloud coverage. These cloud formations can obscure weather patterns and radar technology by sitting on top of a compact, heavily inhabited core at a higher elevation. This cloud core often goes undetected as it veils a central area within it. Our research aims to identify these cloud cores and study their shape using mathematical concepts from point-set topology and shape analysis. By applying homology tests, we can determine if a given cloud formation contains a veiled core consisting of a densely populated area and identify its underlying shape. Our method enables assessment of cloud structure's validity through measures of uncertainty, along with pricing homology tests on cloud data using Gaussian processes. Finally, our approach is demonstrated using real-world data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, where it showcases capabilities for identifying cloud cores and analyzing their shapes.

In a recent study, we have been investigating how the presence of a second plasma layer affects the acceleration of ions when interacting with a laser pulse, specifically one that changes color from red to violet. Our research revealed that when the outer layer is extremely thin and made up of lightly packed ions, it can have a significant impact on ion acceleration. However, the results showed that this effect only occurs when the outer layer is thin enough to be considered a "wall effect". The new research being presented today expands on this by using a larger sample size of electrons, consisting of 20 times as many particles as before, in order to better understand the role of the secondary plasma layer's density. The model shows that when the secondary layer is as dense as the inner layer, its presence has minimal impact on ion acceleration. Nevertheless, when the secondary layer is significantly less dense, its presence causes a decrease in ion energy, leading to a maximum effect when the layer is about 10 times less dense. The research also indicates that when the inner layer is more dense than the secondary layer, the acceleration process is more effective when the secondary layer is present, but the results also indicate that the model may need a larger number of electrons to accurately capture the true effects of two-density plasma.

A fascinating pair of transiting mini-Neptunes has been discovered orbiting the G6V star TOI.1500.8, located approximately 436 parsecs from Earth. The two planets, TOI.1500.d and TOI.1500.e, have dimensions similar to 2.3 times and 2.5 times those of Earth, respectively, and both operate within the habitable zones of their star. By using radial velocity data from multiple telescopes, we were able to determine their masses, which turned out to be around 26 times and 31 times Earth's mass for planets c and e, respectively. Both planets take around 11.8 days to complete one orbit around their star. Additionally, we found that both TOI.1500.d and TOI.1500.e exhibit slight deviations in their orbits, which could be caused by the presence of other planetary bodies in the star system. By analyzing light curves from the TESS satellite, we found that the star also exhibits some oscillations, likely induced by a small, yet undetected planetary presence. Further observations are necessary to clarify the characteristics of the TOI.1500 system.

Using a combination of computational modeling and experimental analysis,
we investigated the behavior of carbon and nitrogen in rutile TiO2.
By comparing interstitial and substitutional sites, our results show that
interstitial C and N exhibit greater mobility and reside in a higher energy
state than their substitutional counterparts.
This difference in energy state is attributed to a shift in symmetry and
charge distribution, resulting in variable bond lengths and the presence of
pi-bonds in interstitial C and N, whereas substitutional C and N maintain
more standard covalent bonds with neighboring oxygen and titanium atoms.
These findings explain the persistent difficulties in detecting interstitial C
and N using EPR in ruby and diamond, and highlight the importance of
considering point defects in materials beyond their structural aspect.

We are searching for signs of the top quark undergoing flavor-changing transitions into a bottom quark or a strange quark. Our investigation focuses on semi-elastic processes that result in the production of a bottom quark, a strange quark, and a single charged lepton, accompanied by a missing energy indicator. Given that the new, highly energetic top quark is produced in association with an old quark, our study considers all possible combinations of decay products, including those where the missing energy is carried by either the bottom quark or the strange quark. By utilizing a dataset of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 36.3 inverse femtobarns, collected by the ATLAS detector, we discover that the predicted rates for these rare transitions are too low to be detected within the currently established limits of the Standard Model. Our study also reveals that the ATLAS detector is capable of identifying these rare transitions, and by setting upper limits on their occurrence, we narrow the possible space for beyond-Standard-Model theories by at least 0.06-0.17 (0.17-0.58) for transitions involving bottom quarks (strange quarks).

The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) is an instrument that will be part of the Athena mission and is expected to study turbulence within the intra-cluster medium by utilizing its high spatial resolution and sensitivity. We propose to test the performance of the X-IFU by observing the known turbulent region, CL0024+1654, which is a cluster that is rapidly evolving and exhibiting significant internal motion. With the X-IFU, we aim to determine its effective spatial resolution and sensitivity in a complex astrophysical environment, even with its high detection sensitivity. Additionally, the X-IFU is anticipated to provide refined mappings of temperature, density, and velocity within CL0024+1654 by leveraging its high energy resolution and spatial coverage, which in turn will facilitate the assessment of its capability to study turbulence within the intra-cluster medium during the Athena science validation phase.

Koployan and Shashkov previously provided a higher bound for the number of colors needed to edge-color a graph F in a specific manner, where the resulting colors form an arithmetic progression with a common difference of r. Here, we examine the possibility of setting a minimum lower bound for this number, depending on the connection structure of the graph F. In particular, we investigate the case when the graph F has an edge that connects two vertices already linked by an edge, and we aim to set a minimum lower bound for the number of colors needed in this situation, assuming the graph F has a specific connection structure. We find that the minimum lower bound we can set is equal to 2, and we establish a more general lower bound of 2.5 for the number of colors needed, depending on the specific structure of the graph F. Additionally, we demonstrate that this lower bound is applicable in situations where the common difference r is equal to 1, and we set an even lower bound of 3 for the case when the graph F is a triangle.
